title: Where food comes from: tracing a meal back to plants and the Sun

summary.text: Almost every food on your plate was made by something alive, mostly by plants. Even curd goes back, through bacteria and a cow, to the grass the cow ate. Only salt and water come from the non-living Earth. Follow almost any food back far enough and you reach a plant using sunlight. Indian families have also kept old knowledge about food, like the six tastes, and science agrees with some of it.
summary.art: A child's steel thali in the middle of the page, with dotted lines running out from each food to where it came from: a rice field, a cow, a mango tree, a beehive, a tiny curd bacterium under a magnifier, a salt pan by the sea, and at the top of every line, the Sun.

intro.hook: Look at your plate at your next meal. Pick one thing on it. Now ask: where was this a year ago? Was it alive? Was it in the air, in the soil, or in the sea?
intro.text: Most children say food comes from the shop. That is true, but it is only the last step. Before the shop there was a farm, a dairy, a tree or a fishing boat. Before the farm there was a seed. This unit follows food back, step by step, to where it begins. On the way, you split open a seed and find a tiny plant inside. You find out what turns milk into curd overnight. And you meet deep-sea animals whose food chain does not start with sunlight.
intro.art: A roti on a plate with a long winding path behind it going back through a shop, a flour mill, a wheat field and a single wheat seed, ending at a bright Sun.

outcomes: I can trace a food back to where it came from: a plant, an animal, a fungus or tiny living thing, or the Earth itself.
I can say which part of a plant a food comes from: root, stem, leaf, flower, fruit or seed.
I can name foods we get from animals, and say what those animals eat.
I can explain that every food chain starts with plants, and that plants make food from sunlight, air and water.
I can run a fair test, changing only one thing, and record my results in a table and a bar chart.
I can describe old Indian knowledge about food, like the six tastes and eating with the seasons. I can say which parts science agrees with and which are still argued about.
I can give big examples from the edge of science. Deep-sea vent life eats chemicals instead of sunlight. Seed banks keep food safe for the future. My own body is rebuilt from what I eat.

terms.meaning: Anything a living thing takes in to get energy and to build its body.
terms.example: Rice gives you energy to run. Dal helps build your muscles.
terms.art: A child eating rice and dal, with a small battery sign and a small brick sign above the plate.

terms.meaning: A living thing that makes its own food from sunlight, air and water. It grows rooted in one place.
terms.example: A rice plant, a mango tree and a tulsi plant.
terms.art: A tulsi plant in a pot with sunbeams on its leaves.

terms.meaning: The part of a plant that grows under the ground. It holds the plant in place and takes in water from the soil.
terms.example: Carrot, radish (mooli) and beetroot are roots we eat.
terms.art: A carrot pulled out of the soil with its thin hairy root tip showing.

terms.meaning: The part of a plant that holds it up and carries water and food. Some stems grow under the ground.
terms.example: Sugarcane is a stem. A potato is a fat underground stem.
terms.art: A sugarcane stalk and a potato with its little eyes, side by side.

terms.meaning: The flat green part of a plant that catches sunlight and makes food.
terms.example: Palak, methi, cabbage and curry leaves are leaves we eat.
terms.art: A bunch of palak and a sprig of curry leaves.

terms.meaning: The part of a plant that makes seeds. Some flowers and flower buds are food.
terms.example: Cauliflower and banana flower are flowers. A clove is a dried flower bud.
terms.art: A cauliflower, a banana flower and a few cloves on a plate.

terms.meaning: The part of a plant that grows from a flower and holds the seeds.
terms.example: Mango, guava and banana are fruits. So are tomato, bhindi and brinjal.
terms.art: A cut tomato and a cut bhindi, their seeds showing.

terms.meaning: A baby plant inside a tough coat, with a store of food beside it. A dry seed is dormant: it rests until it gets water.
terms.example: Rice, wheat, moong, peanuts and jeera are all seeds.
terms.art: A split pea with a tiny curled baby plant next to its two fat food halves.

terms.meaning: The seed of a grass plant that we eat.
terms.example: Rice, wheat, ragi, jowar, bajra and maize are grains.
terms.art: A sheaf of wheat and a bowl of rice grains.

terms.meaning: The dried seeds of bean and pea plants. We cook them as dal.
terms.example: Moong, toor, masoor, chana and rajma are pulses.
terms.art: Five small heaps of different coloured dals on a steel plate.

terms.meaning: A living thing that is not a plant and not an animal. It cannot make food from sunlight. It feeds on dead or living things around it.
terms.example: Mushrooms are fungi. So is the yeast that makes bread rise.
terms.art: A cluster of mushrooms growing on a log.

terms.meaning: A living thing far too small to see without a microscope. Some microbes make us ill. Many help us.
terms.example: Tiny microbes turn milk into curd and make idli batter rise.
terms.art: A drop of curd under a magnifier, full of tiny rod-shaped creatures.

terms.meaning: One kind of microbe. Each one is a single living cell. Bacteria live almost everywhere: in soil, water, air and inside our bodies.
terms.example: Bacteria called lactobacillus turn milk into curd.
terms.art: A crowd of tiny rod-shaped bacteria swimming in milk.

terms.meaning: When microbes slowly change a food by feeding on it. The food often turns sour, bubbly or thick.
terms.example: Idli batter left overnight rises and smells sour. That is fermentation.
terms.art: A steel vessel of idli batter, risen and bubbly, in a warm kitchen corner.

terms.meaning: A non-living material that comes from rocks, soil or the sea, such as salt. Our bodies need small amounts of some minerals, like iron and calcium.
terms.example: Salt is a mineral. Plants take up iron and calcium from the soil, and we get them by eating the plants.
terms.art: A heap of white salt crystals on a black rock.

terms.meaning: How a green plant makes food. Its leaves use the energy of sunlight to join carbon dioxide from the air with water, making sugar.
terms.example: A mango leaf in the sun is making food right now.
terms.art: A leaf with arrows: sunlight coming in, air going in, water rising from the stem, sugar coming out.

terms.meaning: A list of who eats whom, starting from a plant.
terms.example: A cow eats grass. You drink the cow's milk. So the chain is grass, then cow, then you.
terms.art: Three pictures joined by arrows: grass, a cow, a child drinking milk.

terms.meaning: A kind of food that plants make and store, mostly in seeds, roots and underground stems. It gives us energy.
terms.example: Rice, potato, roti and ragi are full of starch.
terms.art: A potato cut in half with a drop of iodine turning one spot blue-black.

terms.meaning: A plant that farmers grow in large amounts.
terms.example: Rice, wheat, sugarcane and cotton are crops.
terms.art: A green rice field with a farmer bending to plant seedlings.

terms.meaning: Food that grows and is fresh at a certain time of year.
terms.example: Mangoes in summer. Carrots, peas and sarson in winter.
terms.art: A split picture: a summer cart full of mangoes and a winter cart full of carrots and peas.

terms.meaning: The old Sanskrit word for taste. Old Indian books named six rasas.
terms.example: Sweet, sour, salty, pungent (spicy), bitter and astringent (the dry, puckery feel of raw banana).
terms.art: A thali with six tiny katoris: jaggery, lemon, salt, chilli, karela and raw banana.

terms.meaning: A sweet juice made inside flowers. Bees drink it and turn it into honey.
terms.example: A bee sipping from a mustard flower is collecting nectar.
terms.art: A honeybee with its tongue in a yellow mustard flower.

terms.meaning: Growing plants and keeping animals for food, instead of only finding them in the wild. People began farming about 11,000 years ago.
terms.example: Before farming, people gathered fruit, roots and seeds, and hunted animals.
terms.art: On the left, people gathering wild fruit in a forest. On the right, the same people sowing seeds in a field.

terms.meaning: A safe store where seeds of many kinds of crop are kept, so they are never lost.
terms.example: The Svalbard Global Seed Vault in Norway keeps more than a million packets of seeds deep inside a frozen mountain.
terms.art: A tunnel into a snowy mountain, with shelves of seed boxes inside.

terms.meaning: A crack in the deep sea floor where very hot, mineral-rich water gushes out. Strange animals live around it without any sunlight.
terms.example: Giant tube worms live beside vents about 2.5 kilometres under the Pacific Ocean.
terms.art: A dark sea floor with a black smoking chimney and red-tipped tube worms around it.

terms.meaning: The tiny building block that everything is made of, far too small to see.
terms.example: Some of the atoms in your dal will become part of your body.
terms.art: A grain of dal zooming into a cluster of tiny balls.

terms.meaning: What it takes to move, grow, keep warm or change. Food carries energy that first came from the Sun.
terms.example: The energy in a banana lets you run and jump.
terms.art: A child running with a banana in hand, a dotted line from the Sun to the banana to the child.

explanations.concept: What food is, and the four places it comes from
explanations.definition: Food is anything a living thing takes in to get energy and to build its body. Our food comes from four kinds of places: plants, animals, fungi and microbes, and the non-living Earth.
explanations.description: Look at any meal and sort it. Rice, dal, sabzi, fruit and spices come from plants. Milk, curd, ghee, eggs, fish and honey come from animals. Mushrooms are fungi, and curd and idli batter are changed by microbes, tiny living things. Salt and water are the odd ones out. They were never alive. They come from the sea, the rocks and the rain. So almost all of our food was once part of something alive.
examples: A plate of idli, sambar and coconut chutney: rice and urad dal (plants), tiny microbes that made the batter rise, tamarind and vegetables (plants), salt (the Earth), water (the Earth).
A glass of lassi: milk from a cow or buffalo, microbes that turned it into curd, sugar from sugarcane, and water.
A mushroom masala: mushrooms (fungi), onion and tomato (plants), oil from mustard or groundnut seeds, and salt.
explanations.art: A plate of idli, sambar and chutney with four coloured labels pointing at the foods: a green leaf for plants, a cow for animals, a mushroom for fungi and microbes, a salt crystal and water drop for the Earth.
explanations.context: This card explains the main idea of the whole unit: what food is, and the four kinds of places it comes from.

explanations.concept: Which part of the plant are we eating?
explanations.definition: We eat all six parts of plants: roots, stems, leaves, flowers, fruits and seeds. From each plant we usually eat only one or two parts.
explanations.description: A plant is one living thing doing many jobs. The root takes in water and often stores food. The stem holds the plant up and carries water. Leaves make food from sunlight. Flowers make seeds. Fruits hold the seeds. Seeds are baby plants with food packed around them. People found out long ago which parts of which plants are good to eat. Some surprises: a potato is not a root. It is a fat underground stem, and its 'eyes' are buds that can grow shoots. Ginger and haldi are underground stems too. Cinnamon is the bark of a tree. A clove is a dried flower bud. Saffron is the thread-like middle part of a crocus flower.
examples: Roots: carrot, radish, beetroot, sweet potato.
Stems: sugarcane, potato, ginger, haldi, lotus stem (kamal kakdi).
Leaves: palak, methi, cabbage, curry leaves, tea leaves.
Flowers: cauliflower, banana flower, cloves, saffron.
Fruits: mango, banana, tomato, bhindi, brinjal, chilli, pepper.
Seeds: rice, wheat, all dals, peanuts, jeera, mustard, coffee beans.
explanations.art: One big imaginary plant with each part labelled by a food: carrot at the root, sugarcane as the stem, palak leaves, a cauliflower flower, a mango fruit and a pile of moong seeds.
explanations.context: Plants give us most of our food. This card shows that we eat every part of a plant, with some surprises from the vegetable basket and the masala box.

explanations.concept: Is a tomato a fruit or a vegetable?
explanations.description: This sounds like a silly question, but people really argue about it. The answer depends on who is doing the sorting. Botanists have a clear meaning for 'fruit'. 'Vegetable' is a cooking word, not a science word.
examples: Bhindi, brinjal, cucumber, pumpkin, chilli and tomato all grow from flowers and hold seeds.
Nobody puts brinjal in a fruit salad, even though a botanist calls it a fruit.

perspectives.who: Botanists, the scientists who study plants
perspectives.explanation: A fruit is the part that grows from a flower and holds the seeds. So tomato, bhindi and brinjal are fruits. 'Vegetable' is not a science word at all. It just means any other plant part we eat.
A fruit is sweet and eaten raw or as a dessert. A vegetable is cooked in a sabzi or a curry. So a tomato is a vegetable.

perspectives.who: Judges of the United States Supreme Court, in 1893
perspectives.explanation: A family of tomato importers argued that tomatoes were fruits, so they should not pay the tax on imported vegetables. The judges agreed that botanists call tomatoes fruits. But they ruled that in everyday speech a tomato is a vegetable, so the tax had to be paid.

explanations.art: A tomato in the middle, with a botanist pointing at its seeds on one side and a cook stirring it into a curry on the other.
explanations.context: Is a tomato a fruit or a vegetable? This card shows that the answer depends on who is doing the sorting.

explanations.concept: Food from animals, and what the animals ate
explanations.definition: Some of our food comes from animals: milk and everything made from it, eggs, honey, meat and fish. Every one of those animals got its own food from plants, or from animals that ate plants.
explanations.description: Milk comes from cows, buffaloes and goats. From milk we make curd, paneer, butter, ghee and khoa. Hens lay eggs. Fish, prawns and crabs come from rivers and the sea. Honey is made by honeybees. They drink sweet nectar from flowers and store it in little wax cells in their hive. They fan it with their wings until most of the water evaporates. That means the water turns into vapour and goes into the air. One worker bee makes only about a twelfth of a teaspoon of honey in her whole life. So every spoon of honey is the work of many bees and many thousands of flowers. Now ask what each animal ate. A cow eats grass and fodder. A hen eats grain. A bee drinks nectar. A fish eats algae, tiny water creatures or smaller fish. So animal food is really plant food that has passed through an animal first.
examples: Ghee comes from butter, which comes from milk, which came from a cow, which ate grass.
Honey comes from bees, which drank nectar from flowers.
Some families eat no animal food at all. Some eat milk but no eggs or meat. Families make different choices for health, belief and kindness.
explanations.art: A cow eating grass, a hen pecking grain and a bee on a flower, each with an arrow to a food: a glass of milk, an egg, a jar of honey.
explanations.context: This card is about foods that come from animals, and what those animals ate to make them.

explanations.concept: Food made by fungi and microbes
explanations.definition: Fungi and microbes are living things that are not plants and not animals. Mushrooms are fungi we eat. Many microbes help make our food, by fermenting it.
explanations.description: A mushroom is not a plant. It has no green leaves and cannot make food from sunlight. It feeds on dead leaves, wood or soil. Scientists have found that fungi are actually more closely related to animals than to plants. Microbes are even smaller living things. Put a spoon of curd into warm milk and leave it overnight. Bacteria from the old curd feed on the sugar in the milk. They make lactic acid, which turns the milk thick and sour. By morning there are billions of them, and the milk has become curd. Idli and dosa batter rise and turn sour for the same reason. Bacteria and yeasts feed on the soaked rice and urad dal. Yeasts are tiny fungi, each just one cell. People in India have used microbes to make curd, idli, dhokla, kanji and appam for many hundreds of years. They did it long before anyone knew microbes existed.
examples: Curd is milk changed by bacteria.
Bread and bhatura rise because yeast makes tiny bubbles of gas.
Idli batter left overnight rises and smells sour.
explanations.art: A zoom: a bowl of curd, then a spoonful, then a crowd of tiny rod-shaped bacteria under a microscope.
explanations.context: Some foods are made with the help of living things far too small to see. This card is about fungi, like mushrooms, and microbes, like the bacteria in curd.

explanations.concept: Salt and water: food that was never alive
explanations.definition: Salt and water are the two common foods that do not come from plants, animals or microbes. They come from the non-living Earth.
explanations.description: Water falls as rain, flows in rivers and sits under the ground. Our bodies are more than half water, and we lose some every day in sweat, breath and urine. Salt is a mineral. Most of India's salt comes from Gujarat. There, people let sea water into shallow fields called salt pans. The Sun dries the water away and leaves white salt crystals behind. Rock salt, sendha namak, is dug out of the ground. It is the salt from seas that dried up millions of years ago. Our bodies also need tiny amounts of other minerals, like iron and calcium. Plants take them up from the soil, and we get them by eating the plants.
examples: Salt pans in the Rann of Kutch in Gujarat, and the Sambhar salt lake in Rajasthan.
A cucumber is about 95 parts water out of every 100. So even plant food is mostly water from the Earth.
explanations.art: Workers raking white heaps of salt in a flat salt pan under a hot Sun, with a glass of water in the corner.
explanations.context: Almost all food comes from living things. This card is about the two that do not: salt and water.

explanations.concept: Every food chain begins with a plant, and every plant begins with the Sun
explanations.definition: A food chain is a list of who eats whom. On land, every food chain starts with a plant, and in water most start with tiny algae. Plants and algae make food using the energy of sunlight. So the energy in almost all food first came from sunlight.
explanations.description: Follow your curd back. Curd came from milk. Milk came from a cow. The cow ate grass. The grass made itself out of sunlight, air and water. Follow fish curry back. The fish ate smaller fish. The smaller fish ate tiny floating algae. The algae made food from sunlight. Every chain on land and in the sunlit sea ends at a plant or an alga, and then at the Sun. There is a rough rule too. When a cow eats grass, only about a tenth of the grass's energy ends up in the cow's body. The rest is used for moving, keeping warm and living. So it takes a lot of grass to feed one cow. Feeding people on plants directly needs much less land.
examples: Sun, then grass, then cow, then milk, then you.
Sun, then algae in the sea, then small fish, then big fish, then fish curry.
Sun, then mustard flower, then bee, then honey, then you.
explanations.art: Three chains of pictures, each starting from the same Sun at the top. Grass to cow to milk. Algae to small fish to big fish. Mustard flower to bee to honey. All end at one child's plate.
explanations.context: This card follows foods backwards, from your plate to the place where every food chain begins.

explanations.concept: What plants make their food from
explanations.definition: Green plants make their food from air, water and sunlight. Their leaves take in a gas from the air called carbon dioxide. Their roots take in water. Sunlight gives the energy to join them into sugar. This is called photosynthesis.
explanations.description: Most people guess that plants eat soil. About 380 years ago, a scientist named Jan Baptist van Helmont, in what is now Belgium, tested this. He weighed some dry soil and put it in a pot. He planted a small willow tree in it and only gave it rainwater. Five years later, the tree had grown about 30 times heavier. But the soil had lost only a tiny pinch of weight. So the tree had not eaten the soil. Van Helmont thought it was made of water. Scientists later found that most of the tree's dry wood was built from carbon dioxide, a gas in the air. A wheat grain, a mango and a grain of rice are mostly built out of air and water, joined together using the energy of sunlight. The soil gives only small amounts of minerals.
examples: A tall coconut tree is built mostly from air and water.
A few months ago, the rice on your plate was carbon dioxide gas in the air over a paddy field.
explanations.art: A willow tree growing in a pot over five drawings, the tree getting huge while a weighing scale under the pot stays almost the same.
explanations.context: Plants make almost all of our food. But what do plants make their food from? This card tells the answer, and how a scientist tested it.

explanations.definition: A seed is a baby plant inside a tough coat, with a store of food beside it. When we eat grains, dal and nuts, we are eating that stored food.
explanations.description: Soak a chana or a peanut overnight and gently split it in two. You will find two fat halves and, at one end, a tiny curled baby plant. The fat halves are its food store. They are full of starch, protein and oil that the mother plant packed for it. A dry seed is dormant, which means resting. It can stay that way for months, or even years, as long as it is dry and cool. When it gets water and warmth, it starts to grow, using its food store to make a root and a shoot. That is why seeds are such good food for us. They are small, they keep for a long time, and they are packed with energy. Rice, wheat, ragi, bajra, all the dals, peanuts, and even jeera and mustard are seeds.
examples: Soaked moong grows a little white root in a day or two.
A whole grain of brown rice has a tiny baby plant at one end. Polishing white rice rubs most of it off.
People have stored seeds for months between harvests since farming began.
explanations.art: A soaked chana split open in a palm, with the tiny curled baby plant and its two fat food halves labelled.
explanations.context: Most of the food we eat is seeds: grains, dals and nuts. This card shows what is really inside a seed.

explanations.concept: You are built out of your food
explanations.definition: Your body is made of atoms. Almost all of them came from the food you ate, and the water and air you took in. Your body keeps replacing its old parts with new parts built from food.
explanations.description: When you eat, your body breaks food down into tiny pieces. It uses some for energy, like fuel. It uses the rest as building blocks. The lining of your gut is rebuilt every few days. Each red blood cell lasts only about 120 days, about four months, and is then replaced with a new one. So the blood in you now was built from food you ate in the last few months. The carbon atoms in today's rice were carbon dioxide in the air over a paddy field last season. Before that, they may have been in a tree, a dinosaur, or the breath of someone long ago. Atoms do not wear out. They just move from one living thing to the next. And apart from hydrogen, most of those atoms were first made inside stars that burned out before the Sun was born.
examples: The dal you eat this week helps build the muscles you use next month.
A carbon atom in your fingernail may once have been in a mango, a cow and the air.
explanations.art: A child eating rice, with a dotted line of tiny glowing atoms going from the plate into the child's arm, and a faint star far behind them.
explanations.context: This card follows food after you eat it. It shows that your body is built and rebuilt out of what you eat.

explanations.concept: Life with no sunlight: food at the bottom of the sea
explanations.definition: Deep under the sea, where sunlight never reaches, some living things get their food from chemicals instead of light. They live around hot springs on the sea floor called hydrothermal vents.
explanations.description: In 1977, scientists dived more than 2 kilometres down to the floor of the Pacific Ocean in a small submarine called Alvin. They were studying hot springs on the sea floor. To their amazement, they found crowds of life there: giant tube worms taller than a child, white crabs and huge clams. There are no plants down there, because there is no light. So what is at the start of the food chain? Microbes. They take chemicals from the hot vent water and use them to make food, the way plants use sunlight. This is called chemosynthesis, which means making with chemicals. The giant tube worms have no mouth and no stomach. Billions of these microbes live inside their bodies and feed them from within. Some scientists think the very first life on Earth may have begun near vents like these. That is still an idea, not proven.
examples: Giant tube worms near vents can grow taller than a grown-up.
Some microbes in soil and in deep rocks also make food from chemicals, without sunlight.
explanations.art: A black smoking chimney on the dark sea floor, with red-plumed tube worms, white crabs and a small yellow submarine shining its lights.
explanations.context: Earlier cards said almost every food chain starts with sunlight. This card is about the amazing exception, found at the bottom of the sea in 1977.

explanations.concept: Six tastes or five? Old Indian knowledge meets today's science
explanations.description: About 2,000 years ago, the Charaka Samhita, one of the oldest books of Ayurveda, India's traditional medicine, named six tastes, or rasas. They are madhura (sweet), amla (sour), lavana (salty), katu (pungent or spicy), tikta (bitter) and kashaya (astringent, the dry puckery feel of raw banana or strong tea). It taught that a good meal should have all six in balance. A festive thali often still does. Today, scientists study the taste cells on the tongue. They agree with some of the old list and explain other parts differently.
examples: A thali with sweet kheer, sour lemon pickle, salty papad, spicy chutney, bitter karela and astringent raw banana sabzi has all six rasas.
When you bite a chilli, your mouth feels hot, even though the chilli itself is not hot.

perspectives.who: The Charaka Samhita, an Ayurveda book about 2,000 years old
perspectives.explanation: There are six tastes. Each one has its own effect on the body. A healthy meal balances all six.

The tongue has taste cells for five basic tastes: sweet, sour, salty, bitter and umami. Umami is a savoury taste, found in ripe tomatoes, mushrooms and cheese. It was named in 1908 by Kikunae Ikeda, a Japanese chemist. Spicy is not a taste at all. Chilli switches on nerves that sense heat and pain. David Julius shared a Nobel Prize in 2021 partly for finding the nerve sensor that chilli switches on. Astringent is a touch feeling, a drying of the mouth.
Some think there may be more basic tastes, such as a taste for fat. So nobody can yet say for sure how many tastes there are.

explanations.art: A thali with six small katoris of tasting foods, and a magnified tongue beside it showing tiny taste buds.
explanations.context: Old Indian books named six tastes. This card compares that old list with what taste scientists say today.

explanations.concept: Eating with the seasons and the place
explanations.description: In every part of India, people have long eaten what grows nearby, at that time of year. Ayurveda books describe how food should change with each of the six seasons, or ritus. This idea is called ritucharya. Grandparents say things like 'eat curd rice and buttermilk in summer' and 'eat til and jaggery in winter'. Some of this matches what science knows. Some has not been tested.
examples: Summer: watermelon, tender coconut, buttermilk, aam panna and cucumber, all very watery.
Winter: sarson ka saag, gajar halwa, bajra roti, til laddoo and peanuts, all filling and rich.
Rice and fish in Bengal and Kerala, where there are many rivers and plenty of rain. Bajra and jowar in dry Rajasthan, where little water falls.

perspectives.who: Old Ayurveda books and many families
perspectives.explanation: Each season changes the body, so food should change too. Eating seasonal, local food keeps the body in balance with nature.

Seasonal food that grew nearby is often fresher and cheaper. Some vitamins, like vitamin C, slowly break down after a fruit is picked. Watery summer foods help replace the water we sweat out. Rich winter foods give energy. But many specific old rules have never been tested carefully, so we cannot say if they are right.
Local, seasonal food often needs less fuel to transport and store. But this is not always true. It depends on how the food was grown and moved.

explanations.art: A circle of six seasons around a map of India, each season with a little basket of its own fruits and vegetables.
explanations.context: Families in India have long eaten different foods in different seasons and places. This card looks at what science says about that old knowledge.

explanations.concept: How people started farming, and how our kitchen travelled the world
explanations.definition: For most of human history, people found their food in the wild. Farming began about 11,000 years ago, separately in several parts of the world. Since then, crops have travelled across the world with traders.
explanations.description: Before farming, people gathered fruit, roots, seeds and honey, and they hunted and fished. Then, in a few places, people began to sow seeds and keep animals. One of the earliest farming villages in South Asia is Mehrgarh, in what is now Pakistan. People there grew barley and wheat and kept cattle about 9,000 years ago. Later, crops travelled. Ragi first grew in East Africa and reached India about 4,000 years ago. Chilli, potato, tomato, peanut and maize all came from the Americas. They reached India only about 400 to 500 years ago, many of them on Portuguese ships. Before that, Indian food got its heat from black pepper and long pepper. Black pepper grows wild in the forests of Kerala, and traders took it all the way to ancient Rome. People in India were also among the first to turn sugarcane juice into sugar crystals. The English word 'sugar' comes, through Persian and Arabic, from the Sanskrit word 'sharkara'.
examples: Aloo, tamatar and mirchi are in almost every Indian kitchen, but none of them grew in India 600 years ago.
Black pepper from Kerala was once so valuable that it was called black gold.
explanations.art: A world map with dotted ship routes: chilli, potato and tomato sailing from the Americas to India, black pepper sailing from Kerala to Rome, and ragi walking from East Africa.
explanations.context: Where did our crops first come from? This card is about how farming began, and how foods travelled the world to reach an Indian kitchen.

explanations.concept: How will everyone be fed in the future?
explanations.description: There are more than 8 billion people on Earth. In the 1960s, India did not grow enough grain and feared famine. Scientists, including M. S. Swaminathan, worked with farmers to grow new kinds of wheat and rice that gave much bigger harvests. This was called the Green Revolution, and within a few years India could feed itself. But it used a lot of water, fertiliser and pesticide. Today people argue about what to do next.
examples: In Punjab, so much water is pumped up for rice that the water under the ground is falling year after year.
Millets like ragi, jowar and bajra need much less water than rice. The United Nations named 2023 the International Year of Millets, after India proposed it.
Seed banks, like the one in Svalbard in Norway, store seeds of many crops in case any are lost.

perspectives.explanation: New high-yield seeds and fertiliser saved millions of people from hunger. Science must keep making better crops.

perspectives.who: Critics, like the Indian writer and activist Vandana Shiva
perspectives.explanation: The Green Revolution harmed soil and water, and pushed out India's many old local crops. Farming should go back to many crops, local seeds and fewer chemicals.

perspectives.who: M. S. Swaminathan himself, later in life
perspectives.explanation: He called for an 'Evergreen Revolution': growing more food while caring for the soil, water and small farmers.
Some try new foods: meat grown from animal cells, insects (about 2 billion people already eat them), or seaweed and algae. Whether these will become common is still open.

explanations.art: A farmer standing between two fields: one of tall wheat with a water pump, and one of mixed millets, pulses and trees.
explanations.context: Feeding billions of people is one of the biggest problems in the world. This card looks at how India solved one food crisis, and why people still argue about what to do next.

agreed.text: Almost all of our food comes from living things: plants, animals, fungi and microbes. Salt and water are the main foods that come from the non-living Earth.
agreed.evidence: Trace any food back, step by step. You always reach a plant, an animal, a fungus, a microbe, the sea or the rocks.

agreed.text: Green plants make their food from air, water and sunlight. The soil gives them only small amounts of minerals.
agreed.evidence: Van Helmont's willow tree grew about 30 times heavier, but its soil hardly lost any weight. Later scientists showed plants take in carbon dioxide from the air and need light to grow.

agreed.text: On land and in the sunlit sea, every food chain begins with plants or algae, which use sunlight.
agreed.evidence: Animals cannot make food from light. Every animal we eat ate plants, or ate other animals that ate plants.

agreed.text: Seeds hold a baby plant and a store of food, mostly starch, protein and oil.
agreed.evidence: Split a soaked seed and you can see the baby plant. A drop of iodine turns the food store blue-black, which shows starch is there.

agreed.text: Microbes turn milk into curd and make batters rise.
agreed.evidence: Warm milk with a spoon of curd sets by morning. Boiled milk with no curd added does not. Under a microscope, curd is full of bacteria.

agreed.text: Some living things at deep-sea vents get their food from chemicals, not sunlight.
agreed.evidence: Scientists in the submarine Alvin first saw these communities in 1977. Since then, hundreds of vent sites have been studied.

challenging.who: Many young children, and many grown-ups in cities who never see a farm
challenging.for: The shop is where we buy it, and where we last saw it before it reached home.
challenging.against: The shop is only the last step. Every food in the shop came from a farm, a sea, a forest, a dairy or a salt pan. Someone grew it, caught it or made it.
challenging.context: This card is about a very common answer to 'where does food come from?'

challenging.claim: Plants get their food from the soil.
challenging.who: Most people, for thousands of years, including the Greek thinker Aristotle
challenging.for: Plants grow in soil, and they die if they are pulled out of it.
challenging.against: Van Helmont's willow grew huge while its soil hardly changed. Plants make their own food from air, water and sunlight. Soil gives them water, a firm place to stand and a little of some minerals.
challenging.context: This card is about an old and very common idea of what plants eat.

challenging.claim: Mushrooms are a kind of plant.
challenging.who: Many older books, and most people
challenging.for: Mushrooms grow out of the ground, they cannot walk, and they are sold with vegetables.
challenging.against: Mushrooms have no green leaves and cannot make food from sunlight. They feed on dead things like wood and leaves. Studies of their cells show fungi are more closely related to animals than to plants.
challenging.context: Mushrooms are sold next to the vegetables. This card asks whether they really belong there.

challenging.claim: Spicy food and worry cause stomach ulcers, painful sores inside the stomach.
challenging.for: People with ulcers often felt worse after spicy food or a worrying day.
challenging.against: In 1982, two doctors in Australia, Robin Warren and Barry Marshall, found that most ulcers are caused by a bacterium. Other doctors did not believe them. So in 1984 Marshall drank a cup of the bacteria himself. His stomach became sore and swollen, and medicine that kills bacteria cured him. They won a Nobel Prize in 2005. Spicy food can still upset some stomachs, but it is not the main cause of ulcers.
challenging.context: This card is about an old belief about spicy food and the stomach, and the doctor who drank bacteria to prove it wrong.

challenging.claim: Old food traditions are just superstition, and only modern science knows about food.
challenging.for: Some old rules have no evidence behind them, and a few are wrong.
challenging.against: Many traditions came from careful watching over hundreds of years. People made curd and idli with microbes long before microbes were discovered. Eating millets in dry places and watery foods in summer makes good sense. The fair way is to test each old idea, not to accept or reject them all.
challenging.context: This card asks whether old Indian food knowledge is wisdom, superstition, or some of each.

challenging.claim: The tongue has separate areas: sweet at the tip, salty and sour at the sides, bitter at the back.
challenging.who: School books all over the world, for most of the 1900s
challenging.for: A drawing called the 'tongue map' was printed in thousands of books, based on a German study from 1901.
challenging.against: The study only found small differences. An American psychologist, Edwin Boring, redrew it in 1942 so that it looked like separate zones. In 1974, Virginia Collings tested it carefully and found every taste can be sensed all over the tongue. You can test it yourself with sugar water on the back of your tongue.
challenging.context: This card is about a famous picture of the tongue that was in school books for decades, and was wrong.

challenging.claim: M. S. Swaminathan and a few scientists fed India.
challenging.who: Many history books and news stories
challenging.for: Swaminathan led the work that brought high-yield wheat and rice to Indian farms. He won the first World Food Prize, in 1987.
challenging.against: Millions of farmers, many of them women, took the risk of growing the new seeds and did the work. Earlier scientists helped too. E. K. Janaki Ammal, one of India's first women botanists, bred sweeter sugarcane in Coimbatore in the 1930s. Credit belongs to many hands.
challenging.context: This card asks who should get the credit when a whole country learns to grow enough food.

big_questions.q: A plant is our food. So what is a plant's food?
big_questions.hint: A huge tree grew in a pot, but the soil in the pot hardly changed. Where did the tree come from?

big_questions.q: If you follow any food back far enough, where do you always end up?
big_questions.hint: Try your curd, your roti and your fish. What is at the very start of each chain?

big_questions.q: When you eat a grain of rice, are you eating something alive?
big_questions.hint: Whole moong and unpolished rice can still sprout. Does cooking change that?

big_questions.q: Your blood is rebuilt every few months from food. So are you the same person you were last year?
big_questions.hint: Think of a river. The water is always new, but it is still the same river.

big_questions.q: Is there any food that is not, in some way, sunlight?
big_questions.hint: Think of salt, water, and the tube worms at deep-sea vents.

big_questions.q: Who brought your lunch to you today? Count every person you can think of.
big_questions.hint: Start with whoever cooked it. Then the shopkeeper, the driver, the miller, the farmer. Who else?

big_questions.q: Some families eat no animal food. Some eat fish every day. Why might people make different choices about food?
big_questions.hint: Think about health, belief, kindness to animals, what grows nearby and what costs less.

big_questions.q: Many people around the world still do not get enough food, even though the world grows enough for everyone. Why might that be?
big_questions.hint: Think about who can pay, how far food travels, and how much is thrown away.

big_questions.q: In 1941, during a long war, starving scientists in the city of Leningrad guarded a store of seeds and did not eat them. When is it right to save something for the future instead of using it now?
big_questions.hint: What would happen to next year's food if every farmer ate all their seeds?

big_questions.q: Old books said there are six tastes. Scientists say five, maybe more. How would you decide what counts as a taste?
big_questions.hint: What would you need to find on the tongue, or in the brain?

big_questions.q: Could people one day live without plants, eating food made by microbes or machines?
big_questions.hint: The tube worms at deep-sea vents live without plants. What would people miss?

story.title: A Field in Every Packet
story.note: The siege of Leningrad (September 1941 to January 1944) is real. So is Nikolai Vavilov's great seed collection at the Institute of Plant Industry on St Isaac's Square, his seed-collecting journeys to Ethiopia, Afghanistan and the Americas, his arrest in 1940 and his death of hunger in prison in 1943. Several of the Institute's workers died of hunger during the siege while guarding the seeds. Accounts differ on how many. In the worst weeks of that winter, the bread ration for children really fell to 125 grams a day. Nina, her mother Vera and the night with the peas are made up.
text: In the winter of 1941, the city of Leningrad was shut in like a box. An army had closed every road. No trains came in with flour. No lorries came in with potatoes. The snow fell and fell, and the city grew quieter and thinner every day.

Nina was ten. Each morning she stood in the bread queue with her mother and came home with a slice of bread no bigger than her palm. It was dark and damp and tasted of sawdust. That was all there was for the whole day. She ate it in tiny bites, making each bite last, the way you make a story last when you know it is nearly over.

Nina's mother, Vera, worked in a grand old building on St Isaac's Square. Inside, it was the strangest library in the world. It had no books. Its shelves held boxes, and the boxes held packets, and the packets held seeds. Wheat from the mountains of Ethiopia. Peas from the valleys of Afghanistan. Beans and maize from Mexico, potatoes from the high Andes, rice from everywhere rice had ever grown. A scientist called Nikolai Vavilov had spent his life travelling the world to collect them. He was not there now. He had been arrested the year before, and nobody would say where he was.

Their flat had no heating, so Nina came to work with her mother. The seed library had no heating either, but at least there were people. They moved slowly, in coats and scarves and gloves with the fingertips cut off. They spoke softly, as if loud words cost too much. Their faces had gone grey and sharp.

One afternoon Nina stood in front of a shelf of rice. She did a sum in her head, and it made her angry. 'There are tonnes of seeds here,' she said. 'Tonnes. And people are dying in the street. Why don't you just cook them?'

Her mother did not get cross. She only looked tired. 'If we cook them, we eat for a week,' she said. 'And then the war ends, and the farmers come to us for seeds, and the shelves are empty. Then there is no wheat, no peas, no rice. Not next year. Not ever.'
Nina did not understand. Food was food. You were hungry, and there it was.

That night, the cold was so bad that her mother fell asleep at her desk with her head on her arms. It was Nina's turn to keep watch. The rats were the real danger. They were starving too. They chewed through boxes and ate whatever they found. Nina sat with a small lamp and a broom, and listened to the building creak.

Then she heard it. A scratching, a skitter, and then a soft patter like rain. She lifted the lamp. A box on a low shelf had been gnawed open, and a packet inside had split. Green-grey peas lay spilled across the floor.

Nina knelt and gathered them into her lap, one by one. Her stomach twisted. She picked up a single pea and put it in her mouth. It sat on her tongue, hard as a pebble. It tasted of dust, and very faintly of summer.
Then she remembered something.

Long before the hunger, in the autumn, her mother had soaked a pea from their kitchen in a cup of water overnight. In the morning she had split it with her thumbnail and held it under the lamp. Inside were two fat pale halves, and tucked at one edge, a tiny curled thing with two folded leaves, like a sleeping baby holding its knees. 'That is the plant,' her mother had said. 'And these two fat halves are its lunch. Its mother packed them for it before it was born. When we eat peas, we are eating the baby's lunchbox.'
Nina took the pea out of her mouth and held it up to the lamp. There was a baby in there. Asleep. Waiting for water and warmth and spring.

She began to count on her cold fingers. Plant one pea, and it grows into a plant. One plant makes perhaps five pods. Each pod holds perhaps six peas. That is thirty peas. Plant those thirty, and there are thirty plants. Thirty plants make nine hundred peas. And the year after that…
She stopped, because the number had become too big to hold.
In her mouth, the pea would be gone in one swallow. In the ground, it was a field.

Nina wiped the pea on her sleeve and put it back in the packet. Then she found every other pea on the floor, even the one that had rolled under the radiator. She counted them twice. Forty-seven. She tied the packet tight with a piece of string, and on the paper, in her best handwriting, she wrote: 47. All here.

In the morning her mother woke stiff and blinking. She saw the box, and the tied packet, and the number written on it. She looked at Nina for a long moment. Then she took a pencil, and beside the 47 she wrote her own initials, very small, as if signing something important.

The siege lasted two more winters. Some of the people in the seed library did not live to see the end of it. They died of hunger at their desks, beside sacks of rice and boxes of seeds they never opened. Nikolai Vavilov, the man who had gathered the seeds so that nobody would ever starve, died of hunger in a prison far away.

But the seeds survived. After the war, they went out from St Isaac's Square to farms across the country, packet by packet. They were sown in spring soil. They woke up and ate their lunch and pushed out roots and shoots, and grew, and made more seeds, and those seeds made more.
Somewhere, a pea plant is climbing a stick in a garden right now. Its seeds came, many generations later, from seeds that lived through that winter. Now it turns its leaves to the Sun.
story.epiphany: For the parent: Nina's turn comes when she sees that a seed is not only food. It is a living baby plant with a store of food, waiting to grow. Eaten, it is one mouthful. Planted, it becomes a plant that makes many more seeds. Most of our food is seeds or other plant parts. Every bit of it comes from living things that keep making more of themselves. That is why farmers have always kept back their best seeds, even in hungry years. The story also quietly asks about saving for the future. It remembers people whose sacrifice was never written in the history books.
ask: Why did the scientists in the story not cook the seeds, even though they were starving?
What did Nina remember about the inside of a pea? What were the two fat halves for?
Nina counted: one pea could become thirty, then nine hundred. How did she work that out?
Why do you think Nina's mother wrote her initials next to Nina's number?
Is there anything in your home that is kept for later, instead of being used now? Why?

games.title: Pass the Sunlight
games.players: 2 to 5 players, or one child playing against the app

printables.title: A long table mat with five spaces in a row

rules: Shuffle all the cards. Deal 6 to each player. Put the rest face down as a pile.
On your turn, take one card from the pile. Then try to build a food chain on the table, starting with a SUN card.
A chain must make sense going forwards. For example: SUN, then Grass, then Cow, then Milk, then Curd.
Say the chain out loud: 'The Sun fed the grass. The grass fed the cow. The cow made milk.' If everyone agrees each step is true, you score 1 point for each card in the chain.
HELPER cards can join a chain where microbes change a food, like Milk then HELPER: curd bacteria then Curd.
EARTH cards can be added to any finished plate for 1 bonus point, if you say where that salt or water came from.
The SURPRISE card starts a chain with no SUN at all. If you can explain it, score 3 bonus points.
When the pile runs out, the player with the most points wins.

flow.do: 1. Lay the five-space mat on the floor. 2. Shuffle the cards and deal 6 each. 3. Put the rest in a pile.
flow.say: In this game, you build food chains. Each chain shows how energy from the Sun passes from one living thing to the next, until it reaches your plate. Every chain must start with the Sun.
flow.kid: Every chain starts with the SUN. Each card passes the energy on. End on a plate!
flow.context: This is the first step of Pass the Sunlight. It is a card game where you build food chains that carry the Sun's energy all the way to your plate.

flow.do: Build one practice chain together: SUN, Mustard flower, Honeybee, Honey.
flow.say: Let's build one together. The Sun feeds the mustard flower. The bee drinks its nectar. The bee makes honey. Four cards, four points.
flow.kid: Practice chain: SUN, mustard flower, bee, honey. Say each step out loud.

check.q: Which card should come between Grass and Milk?
check.why: The cow eats the grass and makes milk from it, so Cow goes between Grass and Milk. 'Sun' cannot go in the middle, because the Sun always comes first. 'Curd' jumps ahead, because curd is made from milk.

flow.do: 1. Take turns drawing a card and building chains. 2. Each player says their chain aloud. 3. Others agree or challenge each step. 4. Score on the sheet.
flow.say: Say each step of your chain. If anyone thinks a step is wrong, they can challenge it, and we decide together.
flow.kid: Draw a card. Build a chain. Say every step. Others can challenge a wrong step!
flow.parent: Good chains: SUN, Rice plant, Rice. SUN, Grass, Cow, Milk, HELPER: curd bacteria, Curd. SUN, Tiny algae, Small fish, Big fish, Fish curry. SUN, Sugarcane, Jaggery. Challenge wrong steps kindly: 'Does a hen make honey?' For the SURPRISE card, a good answer is this. Deep-sea microbes make food from chemicals in hot vent water. They need no sunlight at all.

flow.do: Add up the scores. Then look at all the chains on the table together.
flow.say: Look at every chain on the table. Which card is at the start of almost all of them?
flow.kid: Count your points. Look at all the chains. What is at the start of nearly every one?
flow.think: If the Sun went out, which chain on the table would still work?

games.context: This is a card game about food chains. Every food chain carries energy from the Sun, through plants and animals, to your plate.

setup.art: A long paper mat with five spaces in a row, labelled with a sun, a leaf, a cow, a bowl and a plate.

setup.art: Cards laid in a row on the mat: a sun, grass, a cow, a glass of milk, a bowl of curd.
setup.caption: 2. Build a chain that starts with the Sun. Say each step aloud.

setup.art: A child holding up a dark blue card showing a smoking deep-sea vent, grinning.
setup.caption: 3. The surprise card starts a chain with no Sun. Explain it for bonus points.

games.title: Where Am I From? (a guessing game)

printables.title: A question helper card
items: Did I grow on a plant?
Did I grow under the ground?
Did I come from an animal?
Did tiny living things help make me?
Did I first grow far away from India?

rules: One player takes a mystery food card without looking at it, and holds it to their forehead. Everyone else can see it.
The player asks yes or no questions to work out what food they are. Each question costs one token.
The others answer only 'yes', 'no' or 'sort of'.
Guess the food before your tokens run out to win the card.
Then pass the turn to the next player. The player with the most cards at the end wins.

flow.do: 1. Shuffle the mystery cards and put them face down. 2. Give each player 10 tokens. 3. Put the question helper card where everyone can see it.
flow.say: You will be a mystery food. You can't see your card, but we can. Ask questions to work out where you came from.
flow.kid: You are a mystery food! You can't see your card. Ask yes or no questions to find out what you are.
flow.context: This is the first step of Where Am I From?, a guessing game. You ask questions about where a food came from until you can name it.

flow.do: Take turns being the mystery food. Use the helper card for good questions.
flow.say: Good detectives start with big questions. Was I ever alive? Did I come from a plant? Then they get smaller.
flow.kid: Start with big questions. Was I ever alive? Then smaller ones. Did I grow underground?
flow.parent: Watch for the 'sort of' answers. They lead to the best talk. Honey: 'Did I come from an animal?' Sort of, from bees, but bees made it from flowers. Curd: 'Did tiny living things help make me?' Yes. Potato: 'Am I a root?' No, I'm an underground stem.

check.q: The mystery food answers: 'I was alive. I grew under the ground. I have eyes that can sprout. I am not a root.' What is it?
check.why: A potato grows underground, its eyes are buds that sprout, and it is a stem, not a root. Picking 'carrot' is a good guess, but a carrot is a true root with no eyes. Peanuts do grow under the ground too, but a peanut is a seed, and it has no eyes.

flow.do: At the end, ask which question was the most useful.
flow.say: Which question helped you most? Why?
flow.kid: Which question helped you most? Why do you think so?
flow.think: Good scientists ask questions that rule out half of the possible answers. Which of your questions did that?

items.p: Where does almost all of our food come from?
opts: From living things like plants and animals
items.why: Almost every food was once part of a living thing: a plant, an animal, a fungus or a microbe. Picking 'the shop' usually means only the last step was counted. The shop sells food, but someone grew it, caught it or made it first.
items.art: A shop shelf with dotted arrows going back to a field, a cow and a tree.

items.p: Sort these foods. Did each one come from a plant or an animal?
items.why: Rice, palak, mango and jaggery grow on plants. Jaggery is made from sugarcane, a plant stem. Milk, eggs, ghee and fish come from animals. Ghee is made from milk.

items.p: Match each food to the part of the plant it is.
items.why: A carrot is a root. Sugarcane is a stem. Methi is a leaf. Cauliflower is a bunch of flower buds. A guava is a fruit. Moong is a seed.

items.p: A potato grows under the ground. What part of the plant is it?
items.why: A potato is a fat underground stem. Its 'eyes' are buds that can grow shoots, and only stems have those. Picking 'root' is very natural, because it grows underground. But true roots, like carrots, have no eyes.

items.p: Honey is made by ____ from the nectar of flowers.
items.why: Honeybees drink sweet nectar from flowers. They store it in their hive and fan it with their wings until it becomes thick honey.

items.p: Which of these is NOT made from milk?
items.why: Jaggery is made by boiling sugarcane juice, so it comes from a plant. Curd, paneer and ghee are all made from milk.

items.p: A mushroom is a kind of plant.
items.why: False. A mushroom is a fungus. It has no green leaves and cannot make its own food from sunlight. It feeds on dead wood and leaves. Fungi are a separate kind of living thing.

items.p: Which two foods do NOT come from any living thing?
items.why: Salt comes from the sea or from rocks, and water comes from rain, rivers and the ground. They were never alive. Picking 'honey and sugar' often means sweet things seem different from other foods. But bees make honey from flowers, and sugar comes from sugarcane.

items.p: Milk turns into curd because of tiny living things called ____.
items.why: Bacteria from a spoon of old curd feed on the sugar in warm milk. They make an acid that turns the milk thick and sour.

items.p: In the Milk to Curd test, which katori set into thick curd by morning?
opts: Milk with nothing added, kept warm
Milk with curd, kept in the fridge
items.why: The curd bacteria need to be added, and they need warmth to work. Picking 'with nothing added' usually means thinking milk sets by itself. Picking 'in the fridge' means forgetting that cold slows the bacteria down.
items.context: In the Milk to Curd test, you put warm milk in three katoris and changed one thing in each.

items.p: Put this food chain in order, starting from the beginning: milk, Sun, cow, grass, curd.
items.why: The Sun feeds the grass. The cow eats the grass. The cow makes milk. Bacteria turn the milk into curd.

items.p: What do green plants make their food from?
items.why: Plants use sunlight to join air and water into sugar. Picking 'soil' is the most common answer. But a willow tree grew 30 times heavier in a pot while its soil hardly changed. Soil gives plants only small amounts of minerals.

items.p: Sort these into grains (seeds of grass plants) and pulses (seeds of bean and pea plants).
items.why: Rice, wheat and ragi are seeds of grass plants, called grains. Moong, chana and rajma are seeds of bean and pea plants, called pulses. Both are seeds.

items.p: When we eat dal, we are eating seeds.
items.why: True. Dals are the dried seeds of pulse plants. Soak whole moong and it will sprout a root.

items.p: In the sprouting test, the seeds on the wet cloth sprouted. The seeds on the dry cloth did not. What did the seeds need?
items.why: The only difference was water, and only the wet seeds sprouted. Picking 'soil' is a common guess. But neither plate had soil, and the wet seeds still grew, using the food stored inside them.
items.context: In the sprouting test, you put 20 soaked moong on a wet cloth and 20 dry moong on a dry cloth.

items.p: Draw a seed split open. Label the baby plant and the food store.
items.a: A drawing of a split seed showing a small curled baby plant at one edge, and two big halves labelled 'food store'.
items.why: A seed holds a baby plant and a store of food. The big halves hold the food the baby plant uses when it starts to grow.
items.art: An outline of a split chana seed with two empty label lines.

items.p: Which of these foods is a dried flower bud?
items.why: A clove is a flower bud, picked and dried before it opens. Jeera is a seed. Cinnamon is the bark of a tree. Haldi is an underground stem. Picking cinnamon usually means all brown spices seem alike.

items.p: Match each masala to the part of the plant it comes from.
items.why: Jeera is a seed. Cinnamon is bark, the outside of a tree's stem. Haldi is an underground stem. A clove is a dried flower bud. Curry leaves are leaves. Each peppercorn is a small dried fruit.

items.p: To a botanist, a scientist who studies plants, which of these is a fruit?
items.why: Botanists call any part that grows from a flower and holds seeds a fruit. Bhindi is full of seeds, so it is a fruit. A cook calls it a vegetable. Potato is a stem, carrot is a root and palak is a leaf.

items.p: Ghee comes from a cow. Write the whole chain, going back from ghee to where its energy began.
items.a: Ghee is made from butter. Butter is made from milk. The cow made milk from the grass it ate. The grass made itself using sunlight. So the chain is: Sun, grass, cow, milk, butter, ghee.
items.why: Every animal food goes back to a plant, and every plant goes back to the Sun.

items.p: In the iodine test, which food turned blue-black?
items.why: Rice is a seed, full of the starch the plant packed for its baby. Iodine turns blue-black on starch. Paneer comes from milk, salt from the Earth, and sugar is not starch. Picking sugar is a clever trap: sugar comes from a plant, but it is a different kind of food from starch.
items.context: In the iodine test, a grown-up puts a drop of iodine on different foods. Iodine turns blue-black where there is starch.

items.p: Animals store their food as starch, just like plants.
items.why: False. Starch is how plants store food. That is why paneer did not turn blue-black in the iodine test. Animals store food mostly as fat, and a little as glycogen, a starch-like store in the liver and muscles.

items.p: Making food with the help of microbes, like curd and idli batter, is called ____.
items.why: In fermentation, microbes feed on a food and slowly change it. The food often turns sour, bubbly or thick.

items.p: Which of these came to India from the Americas only about 500 years ago?
items.why: Chilli, potato, tomato and peanut all came from the Americas, many of them on Portuguese ships. Black pepper grows wild in Kerala and is one of India's oldest spices. Picking pepper often means both feel spicy, so they seem like the same thing.

items.p: Why are watermelon, cucumber and tender coconut good summer foods?
opts: They are full of water, which we lose in sweat
They are spicy and warm us up
They keep for a whole year
items.why: On hot days we lose water in sweat. Watery foods help replace it. Picking 'keep for a whole year' mixes them up with grains and dals, which are dry and keep for months.

items.p: Sort these foods into usual summer foods and usual winter foods in north India.
items.why: Mangoes and watermelons ripen in summer, and buttermilk cools us. Mustard greens and carrots grow in winter, and til laddoo gives lots of energy in the cold.

items.p: About how much honey does one worker bee make in her whole life?
opts: About a twelfth of a teaspoon
items.why: One bee makes only a tiny drop of honey, about a twelfth of a teaspoon. A whole jar is the work of thousands of bees and many thousands of flowers. Picking 'one jar' means thinking one bee can collect far more nectar than it really can.

items.p: Which one is the odd one out? Rice, wheat, salt, ragi.
items.why: Salt is the odd one out. Rice, wheat and ragi are all grains, the seeds of grass plants. Salt is a mineral from the sea or rocks, and was never alive.

items.p: In the Milk to Curd test, katori C had curd added but was kept in the fridge. It stayed runny. Write what this tells you, using the word bacteria.
items.a: Katori C had the curd bacteria in it, just like katori A. But it was cold in the fridge, and the cold slowed the bacteria down. So the bacteria need warmth to turn milk into curd.
items.why: Comparing A and C changes only one thing, the warmth. So warmth must be what made the difference.

items.p: In the Windowsill Farm, the seedlings in the dark cupboard grew tall, thin and pale yellow. What were they living on?
opts: The food packed in their seeds
items.why: In the dark, a seedling cannot make new food. It lives on the food stored in its seed, stretching to look for light. Picking 'the soil' is the old idea that plants eat soil, which van Helmont's willow tree showed was wrong.

items.p: Label the parts of this plant that we eat: root, stem, leaf, flower, fruit, seed.
items.a: Root at the bottom under the soil. Stem going up from the root. Leaves on the sides. A flower near the top. A fruit hanging below the flower. Seeds inside the fruit.
items.why: Every part of a plant can be food: roots, stems, leaves, flowers, fruits and seeds.
items.art: A simple drawing of a whole plant with six empty label lines.

worksheets.title: From the Sun to the Sea Floor (challenge)

items.p: Deep under the sea there is no sunlight. Yet tube worms, crabs and clams live around hot vents. What is at the start of their food chain?
opts: Microbes that make food from chemicals in the vent water
Food that sinks from the surface, only
The tube worms make food from heat
items.why: Vent microbes make food from chemicals in the hot water, the way plants use sunlight. This is called chemosynthesis. Some food does sink down from the surface, but it is not enough to feed such crowds. Picking 'plants' means forgetting that plants need light.

items.p: Van Helmont grew a willow in a pot for five years. The tree got about 30 times heavier, but the soil hardly changed. What does this tell us about what plants are made of?
items.a: The tree did not get its weight from the soil, because the soil stayed almost the same. So it must have come from what it took in: water from the rain, and, as later scientists found, air. Plants build themselves mostly from air and water, using the energy of sunlight.
items.why: Van Helmont thought it was all water. Later scientists found most of a plant's weight comes from carbon dioxide gas in the air.

items.p: A cow eats a field of grass. About how much of the grass's energy ends up stored in the cow's body?
items.why: This is a rough rule. Most of the grass's energy is used by the cow for walking, keeping warm, breathing and living. Only about a tenth is stored in its body. Picking 'all of it' means forgetting that a cow uses energy all day, just like you.

items.p: Only about a tenth of the energy passes on at each step of a food chain. Use this rough rule to explain why feeding people on milk and meat takes more land than feeding them on grains and dal.
items.a: When people eat grains and dal, they get the plant's energy directly. When a cow eats the plants first, it uses up most of the energy. Only about a tenth is left in its milk and meat. So to get the same energy from animal food, many more fields of plants are needed.
items.why: Every extra step in a food chain loses most of the energy. Shorter chains need less land.

items.p: The red blood cells in your body now were built from food you ate in the last few months.
items.why: True. Each red blood cell lasts only about 120 days, about four months. Your body keeps making new ones, built from what you eat.

items.p: The Charaka Samhita named six tastes. Taste scientists today say chilli's 'spicy' is not really a taste. What do they say it is?
opts: A feeling of heat and pain from nerves
A mix of sweet and sour
items.why: Chilli switches on the nerve sensors that warn us about heat. So the mouth feels hot, though the chilli itself is not hot. Picking 'just a made-up idea' would be unfair to the old book. The burning is completely real. Scientists only explain it as a feeling rather than a taste.

items.p: Why did Robin Warren and Barry Marshall win a Nobel Prize in 2005?
opts: They showed most stomach ulcers are caused by a bacterium, not spicy food
They proved spicy food causes ulcers
items.why: They found a bacterium in the stomachs of people with ulcers. Marshall even drank the bacteria to prove it. Picking 'spicy food causes ulcers' is the old belief they proved wrong.

items.p: In 1941, scientists in Leningrad were starving, but they did not eat their seed collection. Give two reasons why saving seeds was so important.
items.a: First, each seed is a baby plant that can grow into a plant that makes many more seeds. Eaten, it is one mouthful, but planted, it becomes a field. Second, the collection held many kinds of crops from all over the world. If they were lost, farmers might never get them back.
items.why: Seeds are both food and the future of food. A seed bank protects many kinds of crops, so that one disease or disaster cannot wipe out a food for ever.

items.p: In the iodine test, sugar did not turn blue-black. Sugar comes from sugarcane, a plant. What does that tell us?
opts: Not every plant food is starch
items.why: Plants make many kinds of food: sugar, starch, oil and protein. Iodine shows only starch. Picking 'the iodine was broken' is a good question to ask. The potato test at the start showed the iodine worked.

items.p: You want to find out if the added curd is what turns milk into curd. Which test is best?
opts: Compare warm milk with curd to warm milk without curd
Compare warm milk with curd to cold milk without curd
items.why: To test one thing, change only that one thing. Both katoris are warm, so only the curd is different. Picking 'cold milk without curd' changes two things at once, so you could not tell which one mattered.

items.p: Sort these by what was at the very start of their food chain.
items.why: Roti, honey and fish curry all trace back to plants or algae using sunlight. Tube worms and vent crabs depend on microbes that use chemicals from the vents. Salt was never alive.

items.p: Some people say old food traditions are just superstition. Others say they are always right. What do you think? Give one example that supports your answer.
items.a: Any answer with a reason and an example. For example: some old traditions were clever, because people made curd and idli with microbes long before microbes were discovered. But each old rule should be tested, because some have never been checked.
items.why: The fair way is to test each idea, not to accept or reject them all. Science can learn from tradition, and tradition can learn from science.

items.p: Millets like ragi, jowar and bajra are being grown more again in India. What is one big reason?
opts: They need much less water than rice
They grow only in the sea
items.why: Millets grow well with little rain, while rice needs a lot of water. In places like Punjab, pumping water for rice is making the water under the ground fall. Millets are also full of good food.

items.p: Fungi, like mushrooms, are more closely related to animals than to plants.
items.why: True. Studies of their cells and their genes show that fungi and animals share a closer ancestor than fungi and plants do. That surprised many people.

items.p: In the Trace Your Dinner activity, a child drew these people on her roti chain: a farmer, a tractor driver, a miller, a truck driver, a shopkeeper and her mother who cooked. ____ people helped bring her roti.
items.why: Count each person once: farmer, tractor driver, miller, truck driver, shopkeeper and mother. That is 6 people, just for one roti. There are many more hidden ones, like the people who made the seeds and the tractor.

items.p: The carbon atoms in your rice were carbon dioxide in the air a few months ago. Where might they go after you eat them? Write two places.
items.a: Some will become part of my body, like my blood or muscles. Some I will breathe out as carbon dioxide, and a plant may take them in again to make new food.
items.why: Atoms do not wear out. They move from air to plant to animal and back to the air, again and again.

experiments.title: Milk to Curd: what do curd bacteria need?
experiments.question: Milk turns into curd because of tiny living things called bacteria. Do they need a spoon of old curd to start, and do they need warmth?
experiments.predict: Before you start, look at the three katoris. Guess which ones will be thick curd by morning, and which will still be runny milk. Why do you think so?
experiments.fair_test: To make it fair, use the same milk, the same amount in each katori, and the same size katoris. Change only one thing at a time: whether we add curd, or where we keep it.
results_table: Tilt test in the morning (0 runny, 1 thick like custard, 2 sets and holds)

materials.item: milk, boiled by a grown-up and cooled until it feels just warm on your wrist
3 clean steel katoris of the same size
fresh curd from yesterday, as the starter
a spoon, masking tape and a pen for labels
a warm corner of the kitchen, and the fridge

experiments.safety: A grown-up boils the milk and pours it. Let it cool until it is just warm. Eat only the curd from katori A. Throw away katori B after the test, because milk left out without curd can go bad.

schedule.what: Guess. Set up three katoris of warm milk: A with curd in a warm place, B with no curd in a warm place, C with curd in the fridge.
Do the tilt test on all three. Fill in the table. Say what you think, what you saw and why.

experiments.record: Fill in the table for all three katoris. Then draw a bar for each katori, as tall as its tilt score.

flow.do: 1. Show your child a bowl of milk and a bowl of curd. 2. Ask how one becomes the other.
flow.say: This is milk. This is curd. Tomorrow morning, some milk will have turned into curd. How do you think that happens?
flow.kid: Look at the milk. Look at the curd. How does milk become curd? Say your guess.

good: You add a bit of old curd.
You leave it overnight.
Something in the curd changes the milk.

flow.context: This is the first step of the Milk to Curd test. You find out what turns milk into curd, and what it needs.

flow.do: 1. A grown-up boils the milk and lets it cool until it feels just warm on the wrist. 2. Pour the same amount into three katoris. 3. Label them A, B and C with tape.
flow.say: Each katori gets the same amount of milk. That keeps the test fair.
flow.kid: Wait for a grown-up to pour the warm milk. Each katori gets the same amount. Label them A, B and C.
flow.parent: Milk that is too hot kills the bacteria. Milk that is too cold makes them very slow. Just warm, like a baby's bottle, is right.

flow.do: 1. Stir 1 teaspoon of curd into A. 2. Add nothing to B. 3. Stir 1 teaspoon of curd into C. 4. Put A and B in a warm corner. Put C in the fridge.
flow.say: A gets curd and stays warm. B gets no curd and stays warm. C gets curd but goes in the cold fridge.
flow.kid: Put a spoon of curd in A and C. Put nothing in B. A and B stay warm. C goes in the fridge.

check.q: Katoris A and B both stay warm. What is the only difference between them?
options: A has curd added, B does not
check.why: A and B have the same milk, the same katori and the same warm place. Only the curd is different. So if A sets and B does not, the curd made the difference. Picking 'B is in the fridge' mixes B up with C, which is the one we put in the cold.

flow.wait: Leave the katoris overnight, about 8 hours.
flow.parent: In cold weather, keep katoris A and B warm all night. Wrap them in a thick towel, or put them in a closed casserole. Curd sets in about 6 to 8 hours when it is warm, and much more slowly when it is cold.

flow.do: 1. Next morning, bring out all three. 2. Tilt each one slowly. 3. Score it 0 if it flows like milk. Score it 1 if it moves like thick custard. Score it 2 if it sets and holds. 4. Smell each one. 5. Write it all in the table.
flow.say: Let's tilt each one gently. Does it flow, wobble, or hold still?
flow.kid: Tilt each katori slowly. Does it flow, wobble or hold? Give it 0, 1 or 2. Smell it. Write it down.
flow.parent: Typical results: A sets well (score 2) and smells pleasantly sour. B is still runny (0). If the milk was not boiled well, B may turn a little sour by itself. C is runny or barely thick (0 or 1), because the cold makes the bacteria very slow.

chart.title: Made-up example: how to fill in the table

flow.do: Draw a bar chart together. One bar for each katori, as tall as its tilt score.
flow.say: Let's turn the scores into bars. Which katori made the best curd?
flow.kid: Draw a bar for each katori. Make it as tall as its score. Which one is tallest?

check.q: Katori A, with curd in a warm place, set into curd. Katori C, with curd in the fridge, did not. What does that tell us?
options: The curd bacteria need warmth to work
Curd is made by the katori
check.why: A and C both had curd, so both had the bacteria. Only the warmth was different. So the bacteria need warmth to grow and do their work. Picking 'the fridge makes milk sour' usually means mixing up the cold with the sour smell. The cold actually slows the bacteria down, which is why we keep curd in the fridge once it has set.

chart.note: These numbers are made up, to show what a finished chart can look like.

flow.do: Ask your child to say or write three short sentences. First, what I think. Second, what I saw. Third, why I think it happened.
flow.say: Now tell me three things. What do you think now? What did you see? And why do you think it happened?
flow.kid: Say three things. What I think. What I saw. Why.
flow.parent: This is called claim, evidence and reasoning. Any honest answer with all three parts is good. A good answer sounds like this. What I think: tiny living things in curd turn milk into curd, and they need warmth. What I saw: A set hard, but B and C stayed runny. Why: A had the bacteria and warmth. B had no bacteria. C had bacteria, but the cold slowed them down.

experiments.context: This is the Milk to Curd test. You set up three katoris of warm milk, changing one thing at a time, to find out what the tiny curd-making bacteria need.
