experiments.title: Sprouting Moong: do seeds need water to grow?
experiments.question: A dry moong seed holds a baby plant that is resting. Does it need water to start growing? And how much water does it take in?
experiments.predict: Guess first. Will the seeds on the dry cloth sprout? Will soaked seeds weigh more, less or the same as dry seeds? Why do you think so?
experiments.fair_test: To make it fair, use the same kind of seed, the same number of seeds and the same place. Change only one thing: wet cloth or dry cloth. Count 20 seeds on each, because a few seeds may not sprout at all.
results_table: Longest root on the wet cloth (in mm)

materials.item: whole green moong
a kitchen scale (if you have none, a small steel tumbler to measure with)
2 steel plates and 2 clean cotton cloths or handkerchiefs
a bowl of water and a ruler

experiments.safety: Wash hands before and after. Steam or boil sprouts before eating them, because raw sprouts can carry germs.

schedule.what: Weigh 50 grams of dry moong and soak it overnight. Put 20 dry seeds on a dry cloth.
Weigh the soaked moong. Put 20 soaked seeds on a wet cloth. Count sprouts on both plates.
Count sprouts on both plates again. Measure the longest root. Say what you think, what you saw and why.

experiments.record: Write the dry weight and the soaked weight. Fill in the sprout table for each day. Draw one dry seed and one sprout, the size they really are.

flow.do: 1. Put a bowl on the kitchen scale and press zero. 2. Pour in moong until it shows 50 grams. 3. Write 50 grams in the table. 4. Cover the moong with three times as much water and leave it overnight.
flow.say: A dry seed has a baby plant inside, resting. Let's weigh some, then give them water and see what happens.
flow.kid: Weigh 50 grams of dry moong. Write it down. Cover it with lots of water. Leave it overnight.

ask.q: Will the soaked moong weigh more, less or the same tomorrow?
good: More, because the seeds will take in water.
The same, because it is the same seeds.

flow.parent: Both guesses are fine. Write down what your child guesses, so you can look back at it tomorrow. No kitchen scale? Fill a small steel tumbler level with dry moong instead. Tomorrow, count how many tumblers the soaked moong fills.
flow.context: This is the first step of Sprouting Moong. You test whether seeds need water to sprout, and weigh how much water they take in.

flow.do: 1. Count out 20 dry moong seeds. 2. Lay them on a dry cloth on a plate. 3. Keep the plate in the kitchen, away from water.
flow.say: These 20 seeds get no water at all. They are our comparison. We will see if they sprout without water.
flow.kid: Count 20 dry seeds. Lay them on a dry cloth. They get no water.
flow.wait: Leave the soaked moong and the dry plate until tomorrow.

flow.do: 1. Drain the soaked moong. 2. Weigh it in the same bowl. 3. Write the weight. 4. Lay 20 soaked seeds on a wet cloth on a plate, next to the dry plate. 5. Keep the cloth damp.
flow.say: Let's weigh the seeds again. Then 20 of them go on a wet cloth, right next to the dry plate.
flow.kid: Weigh the soaked moong. Is it heavier? Put 20 soaked seeds on a wet cloth.

check.q: 50 grams of dry moong was soaked overnight. Now it weighs about 100 grams. Where did the extra weight come from?
check.why: The seeds took in water through their coats and swelled up. Water has weight, so they got heavier. A baby plant needs water before it can start using its stored food. Picking 'grew new seeds' usually means thinking the seeds multiplied. Count them and you will find the same number, just fatter.

flow.parent: A typical result is that the moong roughly doubles, from 50 grams to about 100 grams. There will also be less water left in the bowl.

flow.do: 1. On days 2 and 3, count how many seeds have a tiny white root on each plate. 2. On day 3, measure the longest root with a ruler. 3. Write the numbers in the table.
flow.say: Count the seeds that have sprouted. You can tell by the little white root poking out.
flow.kid: Count the seeds with a white root on each plate. Write the numbers. Measure the longest root.

chart.title: Made-up example: how to fill in the table

check.q: On day 3, 18 seeds sprouted on the wet cloth and 0 on the dry cloth. What do the seeds need to sprout?
check.why: The only difference between the plates was water, and only the wet seeds sprouted. Picking 'soil' is a very common guess. But neither plate had any soil, and the wet seeds still sprouted. The seed's own packed food feeds it at the start, so it does not need soil yet.

flow.parent: Moong sprouts quickly when it is warm. In a cold room, sprouting may take a day longer, so keep both plates in the warmest spot you have, such as on top of the fridge. If the wet cloth dries out, the seeds stop growing, so sprinkle it with water each morning and evening.

flow.do: Split one sprouted seed gently with a fingernail. Look at the baby plant and its two food halves, with a magnifying glass if you have one.
flow.say: Let's look inside. Can you find the baby plant? And the food store it is using?
flow.kid: Split one sprout gently. Find the tiny baby plant. Find its two fat halves of food.
flow.parent: The two fat halves are called cotyledons, the seed leaves. They hold the stored food. The root and the tiny shoot are the baby plant. Over the next days the halves shrink as the baby plant uses them up.

flow.do: Ask your child to say or write three short sentences: what I think, what I saw, why.
flow.say: Now tell me three things. What do you think now? What did you see? Why?
flow.kid: Say three things. What I think. What I saw. Why.
flow.parent: This is called claim, evidence and reasoning. Any honest answer with all three parts is good. A good answer sounds like this. What I think: seeds need water to sprout. What I saw: 18 out of 20 wet seeds sprouted, but none of the dry ones did. The soaked seeds got twice as heavy. Why: the seeds took in water, and the water let the baby plant start growing, using its stored food.

experiments.context: This is the sprouting test. You give some moong seeds water and keep others dry, to find out what a dry seed needs to start growing.

experiments.title: The Iodine Test: which foods have starch?
experiments.question: Plants pack food called starch into their seeds, roots and underground stems. Which of our foods have starch in them? Do foods from animals have any?
experiments.predict: Before testing, sort the food pieces into two groups: the ones you think have starch, and the ones you think do not. Say why for each one.
experiments.fair_test: To make it fair, use pieces of about the same size and put the same number of drops on each one. Test every food the same way.
results_table: Where it came from (plant, animal or Earth)
My guess: starch or no starch?
What happened: blue-black or stayed brown-orange?

materials.item: iodine solution from the chemist (povidone iodine, the brown liquid in many first-aid boxes, not the cream), and a dropper or a toothpick
a small cup of water to mix it with
a steel plate
small pieces of: raw potato, cooked rice, roti, raw banana, cucumber, paneer, a pinch of sugar, a pinch of salt and a pinch of besan or ragi flour

experiments.safety: Only a grown-up handles the iodine. Never eat any food that has iodine on it. Throw all the tested pieces away and wash the plate. Iodine stains, so wear old clothes.

schedule.what: Guess which foods have starch. Test each with a drop of iodine. Fill in the table and talk about the results.

experiments.record: Fill in the table. Then make a picture list of the foods that turned blue-black, and say which part of a plant each came from.

flow.do: 1. Lay the nine food pieces in a row on a steel plate. 2. Ask your child where each one came from. 3. Ask them to guess which have starch.
flow.say: Starch is the food a plant packs away for later, mostly in its seeds and its underground parts. Which of these do you think have starch?
flow.kid: Look at the nine foods. Where did each one come from? Which ones have starch, do you think?

ask.q: Which foods do you think have starch? Why?
good: Rice and roti, because they come from seeds.
Potato, because it stores food underground.
Not paneer, because it comes from milk.

flow.context: This is the first step of the iodine test. Iodine turns blue-black when it touches starch, the food plants store in seeds and roots.

flow.do: 1. A grown-up mixes 5 drops of iodine with 2 spoons of water in a small cup. 2. Put one drop on a slice of raw potato first, to show what blue-black looks like.
flow.say: Watch the drop on the potato. If there is starch, the orange-brown colour turns blue-black.
flow.kid: Watch the grown-up drop iodine on the potato. Does it turn blue-black?
flow.parent: The potato should turn dark blue-black within a few seconds. No dropper? Dip a toothpick in the iodine and touch it to the food, the same number of times for each one. Keep the iodine bottle out of reach afterwards.

flow.do: 1. A grown-up puts 2 drops on each of the other food pieces. 2. Wait half a minute. 3. Your child writes blue-black or brown-orange in the table for each one.
flow.say: Same number of drops on each one. That keeps it fair. Now let's write down what each one did.
flow.kid: Two drops on each food. Wait. Write down the colour for each one.
flow.parent: Expected results: potato, rice, roti, raw banana and besan or ragi turn blue-black. Cucumber shows little or none. Paneer, sugar and salt stay brown-orange. Sugar is a surprise: it comes from a plant but is not starch. Salt never came from a living thing. If the paneer turns blue-black, some starch may have been added to it when it was made. Some shop paneer has starch added, so that is a real finding, not a mistake.

check.q: The paneer stayed brown-orange. What does that tell us?
check.why: The iodine still worked on the rice and potato, so it was fine. Paneer is made from milk, and animals do not store their food as starch. Starch is a plant's way of packing food. Picking 'the iodine stopped working' is a good scientist's worry. That is why we test the potato first, to check the iodine works.

flow.do: Sort the tested foods into two groups: blue-black and not. Ask which part of a plant each blue-black food came from.
flow.say: Look at all the blue-black ones. What do they have in common?
flow.kid: Put the blue-black foods together. Which part of a plant did each come from?

ask.q: Which plant parts gave us starch?
good: Seeds, like rice, wheat in the roti, and besan from chana.
The potato, an underground stem.
Banana, a fruit that is not ripe yet.

flow.think: A ripe banana tastes sweeter than a raw one. Where did its starch go?

flow.do: Ask your child to say or write: what I think, what I saw, why.
flow.say: Now tell me three things. What do you think, what did you see, and why?
flow.kid: Say three things. What I think. What I saw. Why.
flow.parent: This is called claim, evidence and reasoning. Any honest answer with all three parts is good. A good answer sounds like this. What I think: plants store starch in their seeds and underground parts, but animal foods do not have starch. What I saw: rice, roti, besan and potato turned blue-black, but paneer did not. Why: plants store starch as food for their baby plants, and paneer comes from milk.

experiments.context: This is the iodine test. A drop of iodine turns blue-black on starch, the food a plant packs into its seeds and roots. You test which foods have it.

activities.title: Kitchen Detective: plant, animal, tiny life or Earth?

materials.item: 4 plates or trays, with a drawing on each: a leaf (plant), a cow (animal), a mushroom (fungi and microbes), a water drop and salt crystal (the Earth)

about 20 small things from the kitchen, such as rice, dal, an onion, a potato, a lemon, haldi, jeera, a clove, tea leaves, jaggery, sugar, a spoon of curd, ghee, an egg, honey, a mushroom, salt and a cup of water

activities.safety: Do not taste anything raw. A grown-up handles eggs and anything breakable.

schedule.what: Collect 20 things from the kitchen. Sort each one onto the plant, animal, tiny life or Earth plate. Count each plate.

activities.record: Count how many things are on each plate, and write the four numbers.

flow.do: 1. Lay out the four plates with their drawings. 2. Explain what each plate stands for.
flow.say: We are food detectives. Every food came from somewhere. This plate is for plants. This one is for animals. This one is for fungi and tiny living things. And this one is for things that were never alive, from the Earth.
flow.kid: You are a food detective! Four plates. Plant, animal, tiny life, or Earth. Every food goes on one.
flow.context: This is the first step of Kitchen Detective. You collect things from the kitchen and sort them by where they came from.

flow.do: 1. Your child fetches about 20 things from the kitchen, with your help. 2. For each one, they say where it came from and put it on a plate. 3. If they are not sure, ask: 'Was it ever alive? Did it grow?'
flow.say: For each one, ask yourself: was this ever alive? Did it grow on a plant, or come from an animal?
flow.kid: Fetch 20 things from the kitchen. For each one, ask: was it ever alive? Put it on a plate.
flow.parent: Tricky ones: jaggery and sugar are plant (sugarcane stem). Tea is plant (leaves). A clove is plant (a dried flower bud). Honey is animal, made by bees from flower nectar, so it is really plant and animal together. Curd is milk changed by microbes, so it belongs on two plates. Salt and water go on the Earth plate. Mushrooms go with the fungi.

check.q: Which plate does a mushroom go on?
check.why: A mushroom is a fungus. It has no green leaves and cannot make food from sunlight, so it is not a plant. Picking 'plant' is the most common answer, because mushrooms are sold with vegetables. Fungi are their own kind of living thing.

flow.do: 1. Count the things on each plate. 2. Write the four numbers. 3. Ask which plate has the most.
flow.say: Let's count each plate. Which plate has the most food on it?
flow.kid: Count each plate. Write the numbers. Which plate has the most?

ask.q: Why do you think the plant plate has the most?
good: Most of our food comes from plants.
Even animal food comes from animals that ate plants.

flow.think: Is anything on the animal plate really plant food in disguise?

activities.context: This is a sorting hunt in your own kitchen. You find out where each food came from: a plant, an animal, a fungus or microbe, or the non-living Earth.

activities.title: The Plant-Part Thali: root, stem, leaf, flower, fruit, seed

materials.item: a big steel thali or tray, with six spots marked: root, stem, leaf, flower, fruit, seed
the vegetable basket and the masala box
one pea pod or one bhindi, to open and count

activities.safety: A grown-up cuts anything that needs a knife.

schedule.what: Find one food for each part of a plant. Open a pea pod or bhindi and count the seeds.

activities.record: Draw the thali with the six foods, labelled with the plant part. Write how many seeds were in your pod.

flow.do: Show the six spots on the thali. Name each plant part and what it does.
flow.say: A plant has six main parts. Roots take in water. Stems hold it up. Leaves make food. Flowers make seeds. Fruits hold seeds. Seeds hold baby plants. We eat all six!
flow.kid: Plants have six parts. Root, stem, leaf, flower, fruit, seed. We eat all of them. Can you find one of each?
flow.context: This is the first step of the Plant-Part Thali. You find one food from each part of a plant.

flow.do: 1. Your child searches the vegetable basket and the masala box. 2. They put one food on each spot. 3. Help with the tricky ones.
flow.say: Look for one food for each part. The masala box has some surprises.
flow.kid: Search the vegetables and the masala box. Find one food for each of the six parts.
flow.parent: Root: carrot, radish, beetroot. Stem: potato, ginger, haldi, sugarcane. Leaf: methi, palak, curry leaves, tea. Flower: cauliflower, a clove. Fruit: tomato, lemon, bhindi, brinjal, chilli. Seed: any dal, rice, jeera, mustard. Cinnamon is bark, the skin of a tree's stem.

check.q: A potato grows under the ground. Which part of the plant is it?
check.why: A potato is a fat underground stem. Look at its 'eyes'. They are buds that grow new shoots, and only stems have buds like that. Picking 'root' is very natural, because it grows underground. But a carrot is a real root, with no eyes at all.

flow.do: 1. Open a pea pod, or have a grown-up cut a bhindi lengthwise. 2. Count the seeds inside. 3. Write the number.
flow.say: A fruit holds seeds. Let's open one up and count how many baby plants are inside.
flow.kid: Open a pea pod or a cut bhindi. Count the seeds. Each one is a baby plant!

ask.q: Is the pea pod a fruit or a vegetable?
good: To a botanist it is a fruit, because it grew from a flower and holds seeds.
To a cook, it is a vegetable.

flow.do: Look at the whole thali together.
flow.say: Which part of the plant do we eat most at home?
flow.kid: Look at your thali. Which plant part do you eat most?
flow.think: Most of what we eat is seeds. Why might seeds be such good food?

activities.context: This is a hunt in the vegetable basket and masala box. You find a food from every part of a plant, and count the seeds in a pod.

activities.title: Trace Your Dinner Back to the Sun

materials.item: a big sheet of paper, pencils and crayons

schedule.what: Choose four foods from tonight's dinner. Draw each one's journey back, step by step, to the Sun. Count the people who helped.

activities.record: Four chains of pictures and arrows, each ending at the Sun. A count of the people on all the chains.

flow.do: 1. Ask what is for dinner tonight. 2. Choose four foods, including one from an animal. 3. Draw each one on the right side of the page.
flow.say: Let's follow each food backwards, one step at a time, all the way to where it began.
flow.kid: Pick four foods from dinner. Draw them on the right side of the page.
flow.context: This is the first step of Trace Your Dinner. You follow foods backwards, step by step, until you reach the place where every food begins.

flow.do: 1. For each food, draw arrows going left, one step at a time. 2. Roti came from atta. Atta came from a mill. The mill got wheat from a farm. The wheat grew from a seed, in sunlight. 3. Draw a little person at each step who did the work.
flow.say: Before it was roti, what was it? And before that? Keep going until you can't go back any further.
flow.kid: Draw arrows going back. What was it before? And before that? Draw the person at each step.
flow.parent: Good chains: roti, atta, flour mill, wheat field in Punjab or Madhya Pradesh, farmer, Sun. Curd, milk, dairy, cow, grass, Sun. Dal, shop, farm, toor plant, Sun. For any animal food, go one step further: what did the animal eat?

check.q: Curd came from milk. Milk came from a cow. What comes next, going backwards?
check.why: The cow made the milk from the grass and fodder it ate. The grass made itself from sunlight, air and water. Picking 'the shop' means going forwards instead of backwards. The shop comes after the milk, not before the cow.

flow.do: Look at the far left end of every chain.
flow.say: Look at the far left end of every chain. What do you notice?
flow.kid: Look at the start of every chain. What is there?

ask.q: What is at the start of every chain?
good: The Sun.
A plant, and then the Sun.
Except salt and water, which come from the Earth.

flow.do: Count every little person drawn on all four chains. Write the total.
flow.say: Let's count everyone who helped bring dinner to our plates.
flow.kid: Count all the people you drew. How many helped make your dinner?
flow.think: Do we ever thank the farmer, the miller or the driver? How could we?

activities.context: This is a drawing activity. You follow four foods from tonight's dinner backwards, step by step, until you reach the Sun. You also count the people who helped.

activities.title: The Six-Taste Plate

materials.item: tiny tastes on a steel plate: a crumb of jaggery, a drop of lemon, a few grains of salt, a pinch of black pepper, a tiny piece of karela or one methi seed, and a slice of raw banana or a sip of strong black tea
a glass of water to sip between tastes

activities.safety: Use only tiny amounts. A grown-up gives the pepper and stays close. If your child has a food allergy, leave that food out.

schedule.what: Taste six tiny foods, one at a time. Name each rasa. Decide which ones feel like a taste and which feel like a touch or heat.

activities.record: Draw the six tastes in a circle. Mark each one 'taste' or 'feeling'.

flow.do: Lay the six tastes in a circle on a plate. Tell your child about the six rasas.
flow.say: About 2,000 years ago, an old Indian book of medicine, the Charaka Samhita, named six tastes. Sweet, sour, salty, spicy, bitter, and a dry puckery one called astringent. Let's taste all six.
flow.kid: An old Indian book named six tastes. Sweet, sour, salty, spicy, bitter, and puckery. Let's taste them all!
flow.context: This is the first step of the Six-Taste Plate. You taste the six rasas named in old Indian books, and compare them with what scientists say today.

flow.do: 1. Taste one at a time, with a sip of water between. 2. Your child names each taste. 3. For the pepper and the raw banana, ask how it feels.
flow.say: Taste it. Is it sweet, sour, salty, spicy, bitter or puckery? Does it feel like a taste, or like something touching your mouth?
flow.kid: Taste one at a time. Sip water in between. Name each taste. Does it feel like heat, or dryness?
flow.parent: Pepper feels hot rather than tasting of anything. That is because it works on heat and pain nerves, not taste cells. The raw banana or strong tea makes the mouth feel dry and puckery. Scientists call that a touch feeling. Your child is discovering what scientists found.

check.q: Black pepper and chilli make your mouth feel hot. What do scientists say is happening?
options: They switch on the nerves that sense heat and pain
They are really very hot, like tea
They have a special spicy taste cell
check.why: Chilli and pepper contain chemicals that switch on the same nerve sensors that warn you about heat. So your mouth feels hot, even though the food itself is not hot. Picking 'really very hot' means trusting the feeling. A thermometer would show the chilli is not hot at all.

flow.do: Talk about which tastes are in today's lunch or dinner.
flow.say: Which of the six rasas are in our dinner tonight? Is any missing?
flow.kid: Think of tonight's dinner. Which tastes are in it? Is any missing?

ask.q: Why might a thali try to have all six tastes?
good: So it is interesting to eat.
Because the old books said a balanced meal has all six.
Different foods have different good things in them.

flow.think: Old books said six tastes. Scientists say five. Who do you agree with, now that you have tasted them?

activities.context: This is a tasting activity. You try the six tastes, or rasas, named in old Indian books, and find out what today's scientists say about them.

activities.title: Seasons at the Sabzi Cart

materials.item: a notebook and pencil, and an outline map of India drawn or printed

activities.safety: Go to the market or cart only with a grown-up. Stay close on busy roads.

schedule.what: Ask a vegetable or fruit seller what is in season now and what comes in other seasons. Mark foods from other states on a map of India.

activities.record: A table of foods for summer, monsoon and winter. A map with at least five foods marked on the states they come from.

flow.do: Before you go, help your child write three questions.
flow.say: We are going to interview the sabzi seller. Let's write our questions first.
flow.kid: Write three questions for the vegetable seller. What is fresh now? What comes only in winter? Where does this come from?
flow.context: This is the first step of Seasons at the Sabzi Cart. You interview a vegetable or fruit seller about which foods grow in which season, and where they come from.

flow.do: At the market or cart, your child asks the questions and writes the answers.
flow.say: Excuse me, which vegetables are fresh now? Which ones come only in winter? Where do these come from?
flow.kid: Ask your questions politely. Write down the answers.
flow.parent: Sellers usually know a lot and enjoy being asked. In summer, sellers often name mangoes, jackfruit and watermelon. In the monsoon, corn and jamun. In winter, carrots, peas, cauliflower, sarson and oranges. Apples may come from Himachal Pradesh or Kashmir, and onions often from Maharashtra.

flow.do: At home, sort the foods into a table of seasons. Mark on the map where some foods came from.
flow.say: Let's sort what we learned. Which foods are for summer, monsoon and winter? Where in India did they grow?
flow.kid: Make a table: summer, monsoon, winter. Mark on the map where some foods grew.

check.q: Watermelon, cucumber and tender coconut are summer foods. What do they have in common that helps on a hot day?
options: They keep well for a year
check.why: These foods are more than 90 parts water out of every 100. On a hot day we lose water in sweat, and they help replace it. Picking 'keep well for a year' mixes them up with seeds and grains. Watery fruits go off quickly, which is one reason we eat them fresh, in season.

flow.think: Why can we buy some foods in every season now, but our grandparents could not?

activities.context: This is an interview at a vegetable cart or market. You find out which foods are fresh in each season, and where in India they grow.

activities.title: The Travelling Masala Box: grandmother's recipe

materials.item: a phone or a visit to a grandparent or elder, a notebook, and the family masala box

activities.safety: A grown-up handles the stove and knives if you cook the dish.

schedule.what: Interview an elder about a dish they grew up eating. List its ingredients and find out where in the world each one first grew.

activities.record: The first page of a family cookbook: the dish, who taught it, the ingredients, and a small mark beside each ingredient showing where in the world it first came from.

flow.do: Your child asks an elder: What is the dish called? Who taught you? What goes into it? When was it made?
flow.say: Every family has dishes that have been cooked for many years. Let's ask about one, and write it down so it is never lost.
flow.kid: Ask a grandparent about a dish they loved as a child. What goes in it? Who taught them? Write it down.
flow.context: This is the first step of The Travelling Masala Box. You collect a family recipe from an elder, then find out where each ingredient first came from in the world.

flow.do: 1. Read the ingredient list together. 2. For each one, decide: did it first grow in India, or did it come from far away? 3. Mark it with a small symbol.
flow.say: Some of these foods have always grown in India. Some came on ships from the other side of the world. Let's find out which.
flow.kid: Look at each ingredient. Did it first grow in India, or far away? Mark it.
flow.parent: First grew in or near India: black pepper, cardamom, haldi, ginger, mango, moong and urad dal. Rice was farmed very early in both India and China. From the Americas, about 500 years ago: chilli, potato, tomato, peanut, maize and cashew. From Africa long ago: ragi, and probably bhindi. From West Asia: wheat and barley.

check.q: Which of these did NOT grow in India 600 years ago?
check.why: Chilli came from the Americas. Portuguese ships brought it to India only about 500 years ago. Before that, Indian food got its heat from black pepper and long pepper. Picking black pepper is a natural guess, because it is also spicy. But black pepper grows wild in Kerala and is one of India's oldest spices.

flow.do: Look at how many ingredients came from far away.
flow.say: How many of our grandmother's ingredients travelled across the world to reach this kitchen?
flow.kid: Count the ingredients from far away. Are you surprised?
flow.think: If a dish uses chilli from the Americas, is it still an Indian dish? What makes a food belong to a place?

activities.context: This is a family interview. You collect a recipe from an elder and discover that many everyday Indian ingredients first came from far across the world.

projects.title: The Windowsill Farm: greens grown in light and in the dark

materials.item: methi seeds or whole moong from the kitchen
2 shallow trays or old containers with small holes poked in the bottom
soil from a potted plant, or coco-peat
materials.qty: enough to fill both trays 3 cm deep

materials.item: a ruler, a spray bottle or small cup, and a notebook

projects.safety: Wash hands after touching soil. Wash the greens before eating, and eat only the ones from the sunny tray that look fresh and green.

schedule.what: Fill two trays with soil. Sow the same number of seeds in each. Put one on a sunny windowsill and one in a dark cupboard.
Water both trays the same. Count the seedlings in each tray.
Water both. Measure the tallest seedling in each tray. Note the colour.
Water both. Measure again. Draw one seedling from each tray.
Measure and compare. Harvest the sunny tray's greens with scissors and add them to a meal. Say what you think, what you saw and why.

projects.record: A table of heights for both trays on days 5, 7 and 10, and a colour note for each. A drawing of one seedling from each tray.

flow.do: 1. Fill both trays with 3 cm of soil. 2. Sprinkle the same amount of seeds on each, about one tablespoon. 3. Cover with a thin layer of soil and water gently. 4. Put tray A on a sunny windowsill. 5. Put tray B in a dark cupboard.
flow.say: We will grow our own food. Both trays get the same seeds, soil and water. Only one thing is different: light.
flow.kid: Fill two trays with soil. Sow the same seeds in each. One goes in the sun. One goes in a dark cupboard.
flow.context: This is the first day of the Windowsill Farm. You grow methi or moong greens in two trays, one in sunlight and one in the dark, to see what light does to food.

flow.do: Water both trays with the same amount. Count the seedlings.
flow.say: Same water for both trays. Have the seeds sprouted?
flow.kid: Give both trays the same water. Count the seedlings in each.

ask.q: Did the seeds in the dark sprout too?
good: Yes, because seeds use their own packed food to start.
Yes, they don't need light to sprout.

flow.do: On days 5 and 7, water both trays and measure the tallest seedling in each. Note the colour.
flow.say: Let's measure. And look at the colours. Are they the same green?
flow.kid: Measure the tallest seedling in each tray. Look at the colours. What do you notice?
flow.wait: Come back on day 5, then day 7.
flow.parent: Usually the dark tray grows taller at first, but pale yellow and thin. The seedlings stretch, searching for light, using up their seed food. The sunny tray grows shorter, sturdy and green, because it is making new food from light.

check.q: The seedlings in the dark cupboard are tall, thin and pale yellow. Why?
options: They are using up their seed's food, stretching to find light
check.why: Without light, a seedling cannot make new food. It uses up its stored food, stretching tall to reach light, and it cannot make the green colour it uses to catch light. Picking 'more water' is a fair worry. That is why we gave both trays the same amount, so water could not be the reason.

flow.do: 1. On day 10, measure both trays and compare. 2. Snip the sunny greens with scissors. 3. Wash them and add them to dal, paratha or a salad.
flow.say: The sunny tray turned light into food we can eat. Let's harvest it.
flow.kid: Measure both trays. Snip the sunny greens. Wash them. Add them to your dinner!

chart.title: Made-up example: height of the tallest seedling in each tray

flow.do: Ask your child to say or write: what I think, what I saw, why.
flow.say: Which tray made food? What did you see? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: Say three things. What I think. What I saw. Why.
flow.parent: This is called claim, evidence and reasoning. Any honest answer with all three parts is good. A good answer sounds like this. What I think: plants need light to make food. What I saw: the dark seedlings grew tall but pale and floppy, and the sunny ones were green and strong. Why: in the dark, the seedlings only used up the food stored in their seeds. In the sun, the leaves made new food from light, air and water.

projects.context: In this 10-day project, you grow methi or moong greens in two trays, one in the sun and one in the dark. Then you eat the food that light made.

challenges.title: The Seed Safe
challenges.problem: Farmers must keep seeds safe for months, until the next sowing season. Damp makes seeds sprout or go mouldy. Insects eat them. Design a seed safe that keeps 50 moong seeds dry and whole for one week, in the dampest place in your home.
constraints: Use only things you can find at home.
It must stay in the bathroom or another damp place for one week.
materials: 50 moong seeds for each design, plus 50 for an open plate as the comparison
jars, steel dabbas, cloth, paper, plastic bags, neem leaves, dried red chillies, wood ash from a chulha if you have it
general: Dry the seeds well in the sun first. Dry seeds stay dormant.
Use an airtight steel dabba or glass jar with a tight lid, so damp air cannot get in.
Keep it off the floor, away from water.
creative: Many Indian farmers mix dried neem leaves into stored grain and dal. Neem helps keep insects away.
Some families keep a few dried red chillies in the rice tin for the same reason.
In parts of India, seeds were stored in clay pots sealed with cow dung and mud, or mixed with wood ash.
challenges.your_turn: Now invent your own seed safe. Draw it, build it, and test it beside the open plate for a week. Count how many seeds stayed dry and whole.

flow.do: Explain the problem. Put 50 seeds on an open plate in the bathroom as the comparison.
flow.say: In the story of the seed library, the seeds were the most precious thing in the city. Farmers have the same job every year. Can we keep seeds safe from damp?
flow.kid: Seeds must stay dry and safe until sowing time. Put 50 seeds on an open plate in the bathroom. That is the comparison.
flow.context: This is the first step of the Seed Safe challenge. You design a way to keep seeds dry and safe in a damp place, the way farmers store seed between seasons.

flow.do: List three ideas together before building any.
flow.say: Before we build, let's think like engineers. Three ideas first.
flow.kid: Think like an engineer. Draw three ideas before you build anything.

flow.do: 1. Build one or two designs. 2. Put 50 seeds in each. 3. Place them in the damp place next to the open plate.
flow.say: Let's build our two best ideas and put them in the same damp place as the open plate.
flow.kid: Build your two best ideas. Put 50 seeds in each. Put them next to the open plate.

flow.do: After a week, open each one. Count the seeds that sprouted, went mouldy, or stayed dry and whole.
flow.say: Let's count. Which seed safe kept the most seeds dry and whole?
flow.kid: Open each seed safe. Count the dry, whole seeds. Which design won?

check.q: Why do damp seeds start to sprout in a store?
options: Water starts the baby plant inside growing
Seeds sprout after exactly one week
check.why: A seed holds a resting baby plant. Water starts it growing, just like in the sprouting test. Once it sprouts, it uses up its stored food and can no longer be kept for sowing. Picking 'the dark' is a common mix-up. Seeds can sprout in the dark, because they start on their own stored food.

flow.think: Seed banks keep seeds very dry and very cold, deep inside a frozen mountain. Why both?
flow.parent: In dry weather, the open seeds may look the same after a week. Then press them: damp seeds feel softer and may smell musty. To copy a monsoon week, sprinkle a few drops of water over the open plate and over the outside of each seed safe every day. A safe that lets damp in will show it.

challenges.context: This is a design challenge. You build a seed safe that keeps seeds dry and whole in a damp place for a week. Farmers store seed this way until the next sowing.

challenges.title: Dinner on Mars
challenges.problem: Four astronauts will live on Mars for two years. Mars has no farms, no cows, no sea, and sunlight less than half as strong as on Earth. Plan where every food on their menu will come from.
constraints: A rocket can carry only a small amount of food, because every kilogram costs a lot to send.
The food must give energy and help build bodies.
You must plan at least one breakfast, lunch and dinner.
materials: paper, pencils, and your Pass the Sunlight cards to help you think
general: Carry dried food that keeps for a long time, like grains, dals and dried fruit.
Grow quick plants under lamps in a greenhouse, like lettuce, methi and potatoes.
Recycle water carefully, because there are no rivers.
creative: Grow algae in tanks of water under lamps. Algae grow fast and make food from light.

quiz.p: Which of these foods comes from a plant?
quiz.why: Jaggery is made from sugarcane juice, so it comes from a plant stem. Ghee and paneer come from milk, and eggs come from hens. Picking ghee often happens because it is yellow and oily like plant oil, but it is made from butter.

quiz.p: Which plate does salt belong on?
quiz.why: Salt is a mineral from the sea or from rocks. It was never alive. Picking 'plant' sometimes happens because salt is found in so many plant dishes.

quiz.p: What part of the plant is a carrot?
quiz.why: A carrot is a root. It grows straight down, stores food and has no eyes or buds. Picking 'stem' often comes from knowing that a potato is a stem, and guessing all underground food is the same.

quiz.p: What part of the plant is cauliflower?
quiz.why: Cauliflower is a big bunch of flower buds packed tightly together. The name even says flower. Picking 'leaf' is a natural guess, because a cauliflower comes wrapped in big green leaves. But the white part we eat is the flower buds.

quiz.p: When we eat rice, dal or peanuts, which part of the plant are we eating?
quiz.why: Rice, dal and peanuts are all seeds: baby plants with their food packed around them. Picking 'roots' happens with peanuts, because they grow under the ground. But a peanut is a seed inside a pod.

quiz.p: Honey comes from bees. Where do the bees get what they need to make it?
quiz.why: Bees drink sweet nectar from flowers and turn it into honey in the hive. So honey is really plant food, passed through an animal. Picking 'milk' mixes up two different animal foods.

quiz.p: A cow gives milk. What did the cow eat to make it?
quiz.why: A cow makes milk from the grass and fodder it eats. That is why animal food is really plant food that has passed through an animal. Picking 'nothing' means imagining milk just appears inside the cow.

quiz.p: What is at the very start of almost every food chain on land?
quiz.why: Every food chain on land starts with a plant, which makes food from sunlight. Picking 'a cow' means starting in the middle. The cow ate grass first.

quiz.p: What do plants make most of their own body from?
quiz.why: Plants use sunlight to join carbon dioxide from the air with water. Picking 'soil' is the old idea that van Helmont tested. His tree grew huge, but the soil in its pot hardly changed.

quiz.p: In the Milk to Curd test, why do we keep everything the same except one thing?
opts: So we know which change made the difference
quiz.why: If only one thing changes, that one thing must have caused the difference. That is a fair test. Picking 'looks neater' misses the reason. A test can be messy and still fair, or neat and still unfair.
quiz.context: In the Milk to Curd test, you set up three katoris of warm milk and changed one thing at a time.

quiz.p: Look at the bar chart from the sprouting test. Which plate had more sprouted seeds?
quiz.why: The wet cloth's bar is much taller: 18 seeds sprouted, and none on the dry cloth. Seeds need water to sprout. Picking 'the same' might mean the chart was not read. The dry bar is at zero.
quiz.context: In the sprouting test, you put 20 soaked moong seeds on a wet cloth and 20 dry seeds on a dry cloth.

quiz.p: Old Indian books named six tastes, or rasas. Which one of these is in that list?
opts: Astringent, the dry puckery feel of raw banana
quiz.why: The six rasas are sweet, sour, salty, pungent, bitter and astringent. Astringent is the dry feeling from raw banana or strong tea. Crunchy and cold are about texture and temperature, not taste.

quiz.p: Why do many families eat watery foods like watermelon and buttermilk in summer?
opts: They help replace the water we lose in sweat
They are only sold in summer by law
quiz.why: On hot days we sweat a lot, and watery foods help replace that water. This is old knowledge that science agrees with. Picking 'make us sweat more' turns the idea upside down.

quiz.p: What did scientists find at deep-sea vents in 1977?
opts: Animals living without sunlight, fed by microbes that use chemicals
quiz.why: At the vents, microbes make food from chemicals in the hot water, and whole communities of animals depend on them. Before 1977, most scientists thought every community of animals depended on sunlight. Picking 'plants growing in the dark' means forgetting that plants need light.

quiz.p: Why do seed banks, like the one in Svalbard in Norway, keep seeds very dry and very cold?
opts: So the baby plants stay dormant and alive for many years
To make the seeds taste better
quiz.why: Water and warmth start a seed growing. Kept dry and cold, the baby plant inside stays dormant and alive for a very long time. Picking 'to kill the seeds' is the opposite of the plan. A dead seed can never be grown again.

applications: Farming: knowing which part of a plant we eat tells farmers what to grow, when to harvest, and which seeds to save.
Dairies, like the milk co-operatives of Gujarat, turn milk into curd, butter, ghee and paneer, using microbes for some of them.
Idli, dosa, dhokla, appam, bread and pickles all use microbes to ferment food.
Seed banks, like the Svalbard Global Seed Vault in Norway and India's national gene bank in New Delhi, keep crop seeds safe for the future.
Plant breeders cross different kinds of a crop to grow sweeter sugarcane, rust-proof wheat or rice that needs less water.
Salt pans in Gujarat and Tamil Nadu use sunlight to dry sea water and make salt.
Beekeepers keep bee boxes near mustard and sunflower fields. The bees make honey and help the crops make seeds.
Doctors and nutrition scientists use what we know about food to plan meals for schools, like India's midday meals.
Space agencies grow plants under lamps, so astronauts can one day grow their own food on long journeys.
Kitchen gardens, terrace farms and windowsill microgreens let city families grow some of their own food.
Scientists studying hot springs and deep-sea vents have found microbes with heat-proof enzymes, now used in laboratories all over the world.
Composting returns peels and leftovers to the soil, which feeds the next plants.

open_questions.q: How did the very first living things get their food, before there were any plants?
open_questions.why_open: Some scientists think life began at deep-sea vents, feeding on chemicals. Others think it began in warm pools on land. Nobody was there to see, and the clues are four billion years old.

open_questions.q: How many basic tastes are there?
open_questions.why_open: Most scientists now accept five. Some argue for more, such as a taste for fat. It depends on finding special taste cells for each one.

open_questions.q: How can we grow enough food for everyone without harming the soil, water and air?
open_questions.why_open: Scientists, farmers and governments disagree about the best mix of new seeds, old seeds, chemicals, millets and new foods.

open_questions.q: Which old food traditions are good for health, and which are not?
open_questions.why_open: Many traditional rules have never been tested carefully. Testing them fairly takes many years and many people.

open_questions.q: Exactly how do the trillions of microbes in our gut help us use our food?
open_questions.why_open: Scientists have only begun to study them in detail. They know the microbes matter, but not yet all the ways.

open_questions.q: How long can a dry, dormant seed stay alive?
open_questions.why_open: Some seeds sprout after hundreds of years, but most do not. Seed banks are still learning how long each kind of seed lasts.

open_questions.q: Will meat grown from cells, insects or algae ever become everyday food?
open_questions.why_open: These foods already exist, but nobody yet knows if they will become cheap, safe and popular enough.

open_questions.q: Is there life in the dark oceans under the ice of moons like Europa, feeding on chemicals like vent life does?
open_questions.why_open: Some moons of Jupiter and Saturn have hidden oceans, and maybe vents. Space missions are being sent to look, but nobody knows yet.

maths.problem: In the sprouting test, 50 grams of dry moong was soaked overnight. In the morning it weighed 100 grams. How many grams of water did the seeds take in? How many times heavier were they?
maths.answer: The seeds took in 50 grams of water. They were 2 times as heavy.
maths.explain: The seeds started at 50 grams. They ended at 100 grams. 100 take away 50 is 50, so they took in 50 grams of water. And 100 is 2 lots of 50, so the soaked seeds weighed 2 times as much as the dry seeds.
maths.context: This is about the sprouting test. You weighed dry moong, soaked it overnight in water, and weighed it again.
maths.why_maths: Weighing before and after, then subtracting, tells us exactly how much water the seeds took in before they sprouted.

maths.problem: In the sprouting test, a child counted the sprouted seeds on the wet cloth each day: day 1, 3 seeds. Day 2, 12 seeds. Day 3, 18 seeds. Draw a bar chart. On which day did the most new seeds sprout?
maths.answer: Day 2. 9 new seeds sprouted that day. Here is the bar chart.
maths.explain: Draw one bar for each day, as tall as its count. To find the new seeds each day, subtract the day before. Day 2: 12 take away 3 is 9 new seeds. Day 3: 18 take away 12 is 6 new seeds. 9 is more than 6 and more than 3, so day 2 had the most new sprouts.
maths.context: This is about the sprouting test. You put 20 soaked moong seeds on a wet cloth and counted how many had a white root each day.

answer_chart.title: Seeds sprouted on the wet cloth, counted each day (out of 20)

maths.why_maths: A bar chart shows at a glance how the seeds sprouted over the days. Subtracting one day from the next shows when they sprouted fastest.

maths.problem: In Kitchen Detective, a family sorted 20 kitchen things. 13 were from plants, 3 from animals, 2 from fungi and microbes, and 2 from the Earth. Make a pictograph where one 🌿 stands for 1 thing. Is more than half of their food from plants?
maths.answer: Yes. 13 out of 20 is more than half, because half of 20 is 10.
maths.explain: Draw 13 symbols in the plant row, 3 in the animal row, 2 in the fungi and microbes row and 2 in the Earth row. Check: 13 + 3 + 2 + 2 = 20. Half of 20 is 10. 13 is more than 10, so more than half of the food came from plants.
maths.context: This is about Kitchen Detective. You sorted things from the kitchen onto four plates: plant, animal, fungi and microbes, and the Earth.
maths.why_maths: Counting and drawing the groups shows how much of our food depends on plants, more clearly than a long list.

maths.problem: In the Plant-Part Thali, a child opened a pea pod and counted 6 peas. Suppose one pea plant grows 5 pods like it. How many peas is that? If every one of those peas were planted and grew the same, how many pea plants would there be next year?
maths.answer: 30 peas, and so 30 pea plants next year.
maths.explain: 5 pods with 6 peas in each is 5 groups of 6. 6 + 6 + 6 + 6 + 6 = 30. So one plant makes 30 peas. Each pea is a baby plant, so planting all 30 could give 30 new pea plants. This is the sum Nina did in the story.
maths.context: This is about the Plant-Part Thali. You opened a pea pod and counted the seeds inside.
maths.why_maths: Multiplying equal groups shows how one seed can become many. That is why farmers always save some seeds instead of eating them all.

maths.problem: In Trace Your Dinner, a child counted the people on each food's chain: roti 6 people, dal 5 people, curd 4 people, banana 5 people. How many people helped bring her dinner altogether?
maths.explain: Add the four chains: 6 + 5 = 11. 11 + 4 = 15. 15 + 5 = 20. So 20 people helped. That does not even count the ones we cannot see, like the people who made the tractor or the cooking gas.
maths.context: This is about Trace Your Dinner. You drew each food's journey back to the Sun, and drew the people who helped at each step.
maths.why_maths: Adding up the people on every chain shows how many hands one ordinary meal needs.

roots.context: We have been following food back to where it comes from: plants, animals, tiny living things, the Earth and the Sun. Now we ask what that tells us about ourselves and the world.

deep_truth.truth: Sort any meal, and almost every food on it was made by something alive. Plants made the rice and dal, a cow made the milk, and bacteria made the curd. In the curd test, warm milk with no curd added stayed runny, because no bacteria were working on it. So a cook only changes food: the food itself was made by other living beings.
deep_truth.habit: We say 'I made dinner', or that food comes from the shop. Cooking and buying are real work, but they only change or move food that plants, animals and microbes made.
deep_truth.evidence: In Kitchen Detective, everything except salt and water went on a plate for a living thing. In the curd test, milk set into curd only where living bacteria from old curd were added and kept warm.

three.who_am_i: You are built out of what you ate: rice, dal, milk and fruit, rebuilt into you.
three.what_is_life: Living things make food and pass it on. A plant stores food in its seed, a cow turns grass into milk, and your body turns both into you.
three.what_is_this_world: In this world, grass stores the Sun's energy, a cow turns the grass into milk, and the milk helps build a child who can wonder about it all.

roots.thread: Most food starts as sunlight caught by a leaf. A wheat plant uses that energy to build its grain. A cow uses grass to build milk, and curd bacteria use milk to build more bacteria. Your body uses all of these to build you. Each living thing takes what another made and builds itself from it, so every meal links many lives into one chain.

teachings.teaching: The young Bhrigu asks his father what is truly real. His father tells him to find out for himself, by looking deeply. The first thing Bhrigu understands is that food is the great reality. From food all beings are born. By food they live. Into food they return. At the end of the teaching, the one who understands sings: 'I am food, I am food, I am food. I am the eater of food.'
teachings.link: In this unit, curd came from milk, milk from grass, and grass from sunlight, air and water. Bhrigu's teaching says the same: every eater is made of food, and in the end becomes food for others.

teachings.teaching: Look deeply at a sheet of paper and you can see a cloud in it. Without the cloud there is no rain, without rain no tree, and without the tree no paper. He called this 'interbeing': nothing exists by itself alone.
teachings.link: Look deeply at a roti and you see the Sun, the rain, the wheat field, the farmer and the miller. The roti is made of things that are not roti.

teachings.source: Robin Wall Kimmerer, Braiding Sweetgrass (2013), the chapter 'The Honorable Harvest'
teachings.teaching: Robin Wall Kimmerer, a Potawatomi botanist, shares the Indigenous teaching she calls the Honourable Harvest. Take only what you need. Never take the first one you find, and never take more than half. Share what you take, and give thanks for it.
teachings.link: In the story, the seed keepers did not eat the seeds, so the crops could be grown again. Farmers everywhere save part of each harvest as seed for the next sowing.

science.text: Almost every food chain begins with sunlight caught by plants or algae. The atoms in your body came from your food, water and air, and they are always being replaced.
Some scientists think the very first life may have begun at deep-sea vents, feeding on chemicals, before any plant existed.

other_view.who: Many biologists, and the Charvaka thinkers of ancient India
other_view.view: Many biologists say eating is chemistry: food is broken into small pieces and rebuilt into a body. On this view, the chain from the Sun to your plate is energy and atoms moving, and there is nothing more to it. The Charvaka thinkers also taught that only matter is real, and that the self ends when the body dies.

practice.title: The Slow Bite
practice.say: Take one small piece of roti, a raisin or a slice of fruit. Hold it in your palm and just look at it for a moment. Close your eyes. Think of the Sun that shone on it. Think of the rain, the soil and the farmer. Now put it in your mouth, but don't chew yet. Feel it on your tongue. Chew very slowly, and swallow. This food is now becoming you. Sit quietly for three breaths.
practice.kid: Hold a small piece of food in your hand. Look at it. Close your eyes. Think of the Sun and the rain that made it. Eat it very slowly. It is becoming you. Take three quiet breaths.

ask: Where does your food stop and you begin?
Can you find any food on your plate today that no living thing helped to make?
If your body is always being rebuilt from food, what part of you stays the same?
roots.art: A child holding a single roti up to the light, and inside the roti, faintly, a whole wheat field, rain clouds and a Sun, with a thin golden line running from the roti to the child's heart.

how_we_found_out.story: For thousands of years, people made curd, bread and idli without knowing why the food changed. In the 1830s, a few scientists looked at fermenting liquids under microscopes and saw tiny yeast cells. But the famous German chemist Justus von Liebig said fermentation was only a chemical breakdown, like rotting. The yeast cells, he said, were not doing the work. In 1857, the French scientist Louis Pasteur studied liquids that were turning sour, like souring milk. Under his microscope he found living cells far smaller than yeast. When he added a few of them to a fresh sugary liquid, they multiplied, and the liquid turned sour. Without them, it stayed fresh. He showed that each kind of fermentation is done by its own kind of living microbe. In 1897, Eduard Buchner found that juice squeezed out of yeast, with no living cells in it, could also ferment sugar. It held enzymes, chemicals the yeast makes. So both sides were partly right: living microbes do the work, using chemicals they make.
how_we_found_out.who: Louis Pasteur, Justus von Liebig and Eduard Buchner
how_we_found_out.wrong_idea: Fermentation is only a chemical breakdown, like rotting, and the tiny living cells in it play no part.
